October 8, 2026




 Venezuela’s Maduro, wife hit with new US torture charges 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — The United States (US) on Thursday filed new torture charges against ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, bolstering a mounting criminal case against the pair held in US custody.

Maduro and Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the United States after they were snatched from their Caracas compound in an extraordinary US military raid in January.

A new court filing shows both are now additionally charged with conspiracy to commit torture, stating that they “inflicted severe physical and mental pain and suffering.”

The alleged goal was to “repress and punish political opposition, silence dissent and perceived dissent, preserve and protect the power and authority of the members of the conspiracy, and intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings.”

Prosecutors detailed apparent instances of unidentified victims, including US citizens, being shocked with electric wires, waterboarded and raped while in Venezuelan detention.

In a 2022 instance, Venezuelan authorities allegedly tortured an American who they accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.

“That torture included electric shock to (the victim’s) arms, legs, and genitals; asphyxiation; beatings; deprivation of food and water; and forced injections of a substance that caused (the victim) to experience seizures,” the filing states.

During his 2013-2026 presidency, rights groups widely accused Maduro of using political repression to cling to power.

Maduro and Flores are slated for a trial in New York next June and are currently being held in a Brooklyn jail.

US prosecutors claim that Maduro used state power to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling, and that he allied himself with cartels to ship tons of cocaine into the United States.

Maduro has denied the charges he originally faced: “narco-terrorism” conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices as well as conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

He has described himself as a “prisoner of war” and said the US military kidnapped him.

Flores has similarly pleaded not guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

She was additionally charged Thursday with “narco-terrorism” conspiracy, the court filing showed.

The pair have asked a US judge to dismiss the charges against them, claiming they have immunity as president and first lady of a sovereign country.

Since Maduro’s capture, vice president Delcy Rodriguez has governed Venezuela as interim leader under intense pressure from US President Donald Trump’s administration.

US energy firms have this year signed a raft of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela, which has agreed to grant the United States control of a huge chunk of its vast oil reserves.

Ousted former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro’s jailed wife Cilia Flores has a “very delicate” heart condition requiring surgery, Maduro’s son told AFP on October 5, 2026, after Flores requested to be released on house arrest. news.title: Chuck Lorre Trolls Trump With ‘Georgie and Mandy’s First Marriage’ End Card
news.text:
Chuck Lorre is using his show “Georgie and Mandy’s First Marriage” to continue trolling Donald Trump after the White House accused him of suffering from so-called “Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

The Season 3 premiere of “Georgie and Mandy’s First Marriage” ended with a sarcastically penned end card from Lorre, featuring a longer-than-usual message where he clapped back at the White House’s argument that he should seek help. The TV creator didn’t necessarily disagree.

“A spokesperson for the White House recently announced that I need psychiatric help,” the message reads. “I don’t disagree. I’m not a big fan of mood-altering drugs or electroshock therapy, you know, ‘Cuckoo’s Nest’ stuff, but I would be up for a chat with a trained professional who gently encourages me to seek out childhood experiences that negatively impact my thinking and behavior.”

It continued: “(A possible culprit could be weekly atomic bomb drills in grade school. This involved hiding under my desk to avoid being cut to ribbons from the classroom windows imploding.) It might also be worth investigating if toxins in my environment bear any responsibility for my ‘derangement.’ (Can’t ignore all those mesothelioma commercials.) Regardless of how we proceed, I do appreciate this very public concern for my mental health. It’s comforting to know my government is looking out for me.”

While accepting the Founders Angel Award at Project Angel Food back in late September, “The Big Bang Theory” creator launched straight into a number jokes and barbs about the president, which sparked the White House’s ire.

“Sure, I’d love to stand here and talk about my deep yearning for a more compassionate government, one that prioritizes the health and welfare of its citizens,” Lorre said, as reported by the Daily Beast. “But the burden of my profession demands that I take this opportunity to say a few words about that bloated orange piece of s–t in the White House.”

He continued: “I’d love to express my gratitude to all the people who’ve devoted their lives to making Project Angel Food an oasis for those in need. That would be my preference. But because I’m a comedy writer, I have no choice but to explain how I wake up every morning to turn on CNN to see if the president of the United States had a heart attack while straining to take a dump.”

The White House jumped in days later claiming Lorre was suffering from an acute case of Trump Derangement Syndrome and that he should seek help immediately.

 “Chuck Lorre should immediately seek psychiatric help to treat his severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital.
news.summary:
"I do appreciate this very public concern for my mental health," the TV creator says after the White House accused him of "Trump Derangement Syndrome"

news.title: Trump says FBI may look into Nolan Wells' death
news.text:
President Donald Trump said that he might have federal investigators look into the death of Mississippi teenager Nolan Wells, who disappeared during a July 4 boat trip with friends.

Wells, 18, was found dead July 6 on the northwest end of the isolated Horn Island, days after he was reported missing. State and private autopsies listed Wells' cause and manner of death as undetermined, and a grand jury unanimously declined to indict anyone for a crime in connection with his death.

The case dredged up fears that Black Americans aren't safe among groups of predominantly White people and that their deaths won't be investigated properly. Wells' family hired civil rights attorney Ben Crump to lead an independent investigation, citing a lack of confidence in law enforcement officials in a state with a history of extreme racial violence.

Reporters asked the president at the White House on Oct. 7 whether he planned to have the FBI conduct its own investigation.

"Well, we're ​looking at that. Yes, we are," he replied, according to a Reuters report.

Calls for federal investigation into Wells' death grow

Trump's response comes after the Congressional Black Caucus wrote a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel calling for a deeper look into the case in August. The NAACP and the Rev. Al Sharpton supported the demand.

On Oct. 5, Wells' parents, Christine and Elmore Wonsley, renewed the calls for a federal investigation into his death. U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), U.S. Rep. Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.), Stop AAPI Hate and the National Asian Pacific American Women's Forum also spoke out and echoed demands for a federal investigation.

The Department of Justice said in a statement to People magazine on Oct. 6 that federal officials assisted with the initial investigation and agreed with the determination made by local authorities. The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment from USA TODAY about whether they will investigate Wells' death further.

Crump, who has previously called for the DOJ to investigate, welcomed Trump's comments.

“Sunday will mark 100 days since we have been looking into the death of Nolan Wells, so when President Trump responds to news reporters that ‘we’re looking into it,’ we believe that carries more weight than the response given by the FBI," Crump said in a statement. "Our team stands ready to work with the federal government to ensure Nolan's death is investigated to the fullest extent.”

What the grand jury investigation into Nolan Wells' death found

The grand jury concluded in its report released in September that Wells chose to remain on Horn Island to socialize, which was not uncommon for people to do on holidays. There was no evidence he got into any physical altercation or argument on July 4, the grand jury said.

The report said that "drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion," meaning other causes must be ruled out. Bruising found on his head was not a fatal injury and there was no evidence of any fatal injury, the grand jury said.

"The Grand Jury finds that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells' body is consistent with drowning," the report said.

Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath dismissed speculation that race played a role in Wells' death and accused Crump's team of allowing false narratives about the case to spread

"The narrative that three White boys and a Black boy went to an island, and only three White friends returned, spread like wildfire," she said. "This was false."

The Wonsleys and their attorney have pushed back on the notion that Wells accidentally drowned and demanded further investigation. Crump has said it remains unclear why Wells remained on the island instead of going back with his friends, how he ended up in the water and what caused the bruising on the back of his head.

"Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath will have you accept that Nolan Wells' death can be summarized in three words: We'll never know," Crump said. "But Nolan's family offers three other words: We'll never stop."

Contributing: Reuters

news.title: Jane Doe's texts to 'Cornell 7' frat boy after alleged rape are revealed: 'My memory is super clouded... but none of it was illegal'

Jane Doe's texts to 'Cornell 7' frat boy after alleged rape are revealed: 'My memory is super clouded... but none of it was illegal'

GRAPHIC CONTENT WARNING 

By RACHEL BOWMAN, US SENIOR NEWS REPORTER

Published: 20:16 BST, 8 October 2026 | Updated: 20:37 BST, 8 October 2026

Jane Doe texted one of the 'Cornell 7' fraternity brothers she has accused of a horrific gang rape, saying her memory was clouded but 'none of the sexual stuff was illegal.'

The woman, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month, claiming she was coerced into taking drugs and sexually assaulted by seven members of Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity at an off-campus house on October 20, 2024.

Text messages obtained by TMZ showed that Jane Doe and one of the men she accused, Jonathan Newell, texted the next day, October 21, 2025.

Newell reached out to Jane Doe and wrote: 'I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night. My memory is kinda fuzzy abt [sic] a lot of it.'

He then said that both he and another accused fraternity brother, Matthew Ingalls, felt terrible for being too intoxicated to 'shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.' 

Jane Doe responded: 'Aw jonathan i really appreciate this text. my memories are super clouded too. i think we were all way to f**king drunk and high. 

 'At the end of the day non [sic] of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly I really liked being w u and matt.'

Jane Doe then reported the alleged rape three weeks after the incident, but prosecutors determined there was 'insufficient evidence' to bring criminal sexual assault charges, and the seven men have denied the accusations against them. 

Cornell launched a Title IX investigation into the students in 2025, and the university shut down the fraternity.

One of the men allegedly posted to the fraternity's active-members Snapchat group saying that there was 'free p***y' upstairs, referring to Doe, according to the filing, which included an image of the purported chat

Newell was subsequently expelled from Cornell by a Title IX investigation, and the Daily Mail revealed this week that Newell has also since been kicked out of Nova Southeastern University in Florida. 

In the text message, Newell told Jane Doe she is an 'amazing person' and that he hoped she was not 'catching as much heat from this' as the fraternity brothers were.

Jane Doe brushed off concerns from other people about their 'gangbang' and said they should not feel ashamed. 

'So anything anyone has to say about the gamgbang [sic] is out of their jurisdiction. I don't think we should feel any shame for the part. our body our choice,' she allegedly wrote.

Internal Cornell paperwork detailed by The New York Times on Thursday found that Newell was meant to work the night of her alleged attack as a sober safety monitor.

Newell was meant to be a 'trained event monitor' at the party who would remain sober and wear distinctive clothing, so their fellow partygoers could easily identify them in the event of an emergency. 

Although Newell was listed as one of the sober monitors, the woman alleged in the civil lawsuit last month that he and his fraternity brothers plied her with drugs and alcohol before the alleged rape.

Jane Doe's civil lawsuit alleged that she was sexually assaulted over a brutal seven-hour ordeal, during which time Newell also sent a Snapchat message to his fraternity inviting them to join.

Jane Doe's lawsuit sparked national outrage over how authorities handled the case

Newell denied the allegations and told investigators that he had consensual sexual activity with Jane Doe on the night, and the new records show he claimed not to remember sending the Snapchat message.

Jane Doe's lawsuit sparked national outrage over how authorities handled the case, and New York Attorney General Letitia James has since opened an 'active criminal investigation' into the allegations.

Cornell has hired Sally Yates, a former Obama-appointed justice official who was infamously fired by President Donald Trump, to investigate its response to gang rape allegations.
news.summary: Jane Doe texted one of the 'Cornell 7' fraternity brothers she has accused of a horrific gang rape, saying her memory was clouded but 'none of the sexual stuff was illegal.'

news.title: ‘Secure our security through our own strength’: South Korea tests its first homegrown hypersonic weapon a week after North Korea’s own launch
news.text:
There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it’s a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defense capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.

The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and maneuvered both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theater of operations.”

Lee stressed that South Korea “must secure our security through our own strength,” and also inspected the country’s most powerful Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile on Thursday, his office said. It did not mention any direct comments by Lee on the North.

Tensions between the Koreas have increased in recent weeks after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border.

The South’s military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South’s demands for an apology.

North Korea has also stepped up weapons testing activity as its leader Kim Jong Un expands his military nuclear program while taking an increasingly hard line toward Seoul.

Kim has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy that broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for its denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favors engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric toward the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts.

Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea’s conventional defense capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States, which unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with the South in August, with Trump citing his “very good relationship” with Kim.

In its latest weapons test on Oct. 3, North Korea launched what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that it said flew more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). Japan said the missile landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.

South Korea said it detected the missile flying more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), while Japan’s Defense Ministry said it assessed that the missile flew about 680 kilometers (422 miles).

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, claimed the differing flight estimates by the two U.S. allies showed they are incapable of properly tracking such a missile during its flight and would therefore not be able to intercept it.
news.summary: There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.
news.author: Kim Tong-Hyung,The Associated Press

news.title: Carney says Canada's future up to Canadians after Musk voices support for separatism
news.text:
Carney says Canada's future up to Canadians after Musk voices support for separatism

Carney reacts to Musk

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded Thursday to tech industrialist Elon Musk's endorsement of provincial separation movements by saying Canada's future will be decided by its citizens — not by large U.S. tech firms.

Speaking at a news conference in Sherbrooke, Que., Carney said Canadians can live their lives in Quebec and across the country "free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."

"The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec," he said in reply to questions from a reporter about Musk's comments.

He added those priorities include affordability, social justice and building a strong Quebec within a more independent and prosperous Canada.

Musk argued on his X platform on Wednesday that Quebec should leave the federation, and that Alberta and Saskatchewan should follow suit.

"Quebec should separate," Musk said. "They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too."

On Wednesday, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe replied to Musk's post with a terse rebuttal: "No."

Carney recently announced a major $2.3-billion contract with Telesat for low-Earth orbit satellite connectivity for the military.

That service has aspirations to become a direct commercial challenger to Musk's Starlink, which dominates the global market for low-Earth orbit satellite internet service.

Quebec voters elected a separatist government on Monday by granting the Parti Québécois a minority government.

PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon pledged during the election that his party would not hold a referendum on separation while U.S. President Donald Trump remains in office.

Carney has sought to use his ambitious economic agenda as an olive branch to the province and its new government, vowing Quebec will benefit from cooperative federalism.

The prime minister said in French on Thursday that he and St-Pierre Plamondon had a "cordial" first conversation this week that touched on "great investments here in Quebec," immigration and other matters.

But the PQ has opposed the Carney government's plans for the Alto project, a proposed high-speed rail link between Quebec and Ontario, raising questions about its viability.

Carney talked up the Alto project on Thursday when asked about its future prospects. He said in French it will create tens of thousands of jobs in the province and that he will work with the new provincial government to advance the project.

Alberta holds its own separation referendum in less than two weeks on Oct. 19.

Speaking in Edmonton on Thursday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith argued that separatist sentiment in her province has weakened because she and Carney have addressed the "very real issues that were frustrating Albertans."

"The federal government has changed. Their approach to us has changed and they're willing to work together on addressing those issues," she said.

news.title: Hurricane Isaias update: Gulf Coast braces for life-threatening storm surge
news.text:
Mandatory evacuations have been announced and schools closed across parts of coastal Florida after Isaias intensified into the Atlantic season's first hurricane, advancing towards the US Gulf Coast Thursday, the National Hurricane Center said.

Forecasters warned that Isaias could deliver destructive hurricane-force winds to the Florida Panhandle, alongside southern Alabama and southern Mississippi. 

“A life-threatening storm surge is expected from the Mouth of the Mississippi River to Suwannee, Florida. Residents in the warning area should follow advice given by local officials and evacuate immediately if told to do so,” the National Weather Service said Thursday. 

“Damaging wind gusts are possible over much of central and northern Alabama and portions of western and northern Georgia, especially in areas of higher terrain,’ the NWS continued. 

It could also cause a life-threatening storm surge along areas of the northern Gulf Coast, while potentially bringing heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) across the central Gulf Coast, according to the hurricane center.

An advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center said the cyclone’s center was positioned approximately 740 kilometres (460 miles) south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, carrying maximum sustained winds of around 121 kph (75 mph).

After the storm initially formed earlier Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening. 

Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.

The National Weather Service told communities from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Gulf County, Florida, to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages.”

Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, nearly tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.

The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.

Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.

One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.

Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the U.S.

As of Wednesday about 25 per cent of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.

With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.

As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.

In Alabama, the cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.

Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground. Her family planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.

“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.

In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.

“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
news.summary: Forecasters warned Isaias could deliver destructive hurricane-force winds
news.author: Dave Collins and Hallie Golden,R.j. Rico

news.title: Most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast, a new AP-NORC poll finds
news.text: Worries around artificial intelligence cross party lines, with the vast majority of Americans saying the U.S. government should prioritize keeping AI under human control and protecting workers.A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that most Americans, 64%, think AI is developing “too fast,” while 27% say its development has been “about right” and only 8% say it's moving “too slow.”The risk that powerful AI models could evade human control and hurt humanity, once the stuff of science fiction, has been emerging as a more pressing concern. Even leaders of the companies that are developing frontier AI models are calling for a slowdown so that government regulation can catch up. President Donald Trump has pushed back against slowing down AI development because of concerns that China will gain an advantage with the technology. Data centers powering AI projects have also taken a prominent role in major political races as the midterm elections approach.About 8 in 10 U.S. adults say it's “extremely” or “very” important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control, and they are about as likely to want the government to prioritize protecting the country's workforce. Most U.S. adults also think minimizing environmental harm and growing the U.S. economy are highly important. About half say this about promoting technological innovation, and slightly fewer say that about competing with China.There's bipartisan concern about the speed of AI's development, but few Americans think either major political party has an advantage in handling artificial intelligence. Trump, a Republican, also gets a low rating on his handling of the issue, with 67% of U.S. adults disapproving of his performance on AI.Stephanie Stewart, a junior-high science teacher in Sunset, Utah, said she is frustrated by the president’s opposition to AI regulation.“There is no handling of the issue except for we’re just going to allow these companies to do whatever they want, and we’re not going to regulate them,” said Stewart, 53.RELATED STORY | Most Americans use AI, but few are willing to pay for itMost say protecting workers should be a priority for the governmentRon Theusch, a truck driver who lives in rural Alden, Minnesota, said his No. 1 concern with AI is the potential loss of jobs — including his own.“I can just see a train of self-driving trucks 24/7, just running up and down I-35, loading and unloading. I can just see that happening,” said Theusch, 58.Most Democrats and Republicans agree on the importance of protecting workers and keeping AI under human control, the poll found.“There was a movie called ‘Terminator,’ where the robots came back and killed everybody,” Theusch said. “People relate to that ... I don’t know where it’s going to land. I really don’t have anything I can do to control it, you know. It’s going to evolve.”There's less consensus about the importance of other priorities when it comes to AI. Republicans are more likely than Democrats to say it’s highly important to grow the U.S. economy and to compete with other countries like China. Democrats, on the other hand, are more likely to say it’s at least “very” important to minimize environmental harm.“I don’t understand how, because they’re doing something as well as us, that we can’t be more human about it and more humane about it than just to say, ‘Well, they’re doing it, so we have to do it,’” Stewart said of U.S. competition with China.And while about three-quarters of Democrats say AI is developing “too fast,” only about half of Republicans share that worry. People under 30 years old also express higher levels of concern than people 60 or older, the survey found.“I think I have all the normal concerns, right? I think it’s wonderful for certain applications, but I also feel like it will be overused and can create a lack of personal connections. It can make people lazy because information is just given to them without really having to research things on their own,” said Kelly Opp, a 62-year-old Republican in Albuquerque, New Mexico.“Like everything else, once you get that ball rolling, it progresses fast on its own, but I think that it will continue to keep progressing. So the speed doesn’t really bother me,” she said.RELATED STORY | Trump administration accuses Microsoft of fraud, bars it from green card programAmericans have little confidence in Democrats or Republicans on AIAs a teacher, Stewart regularly uses AI to help with her work, including with creating assignments or assisting with tests. But she is deeply concerned about AI's effects on children.“You’ve got to protect kids. You’ve got to protect teens. You've got to protect privacy ... we need to try to do something,” she said.Americans have little trust in either party when it comes to the handling of AI issues. About 4 in 10 Americans say they don’t trust either the Democratic Party or the Republican Party on AI, according to the poll, while nearly 2 in 10 trust both parties equally, and the rest are split between trusting the Republicans and the Democrats.Even people who identify with the parties are ambivalent about their ability to handle the issue. Only about half of Republicans and Democrats say their party is better equipped to handle AI issues, and roughly 3 in 10 in each case say neither party is.“I am kind of moderate. And I see that there’s good on both sides," said Stewart. "Anyone back in Washington is weak on doing anything for anyone but themselves right now. So, no, I don’t think the Democrats would do a better job per se. Maybe they would definitely tout it. But until I see anything coming from anyone, I’m going to be like, ‘Yeah, no. You’re all just sitting there.’”
news.summary: Most Americans, 64%, think AI is developing “too fast,” according to a new AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
news.author: AP via Scripps News Group

news.title: Iran war could force Israel to postpone election, IDF chief tells US officials
news.text: IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has told senior U.S. government and military officials that a renewed military escalation with Iran could force Israel to postpone its general election, currently scheduled for October 27, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Zamir raised serious concerns about the security and political consequences of another direct confrontation with Tehran, warning that a major outbreak of fighting so close to the vote could make holding the election on schedule impossible. Israel’s security chiefs have already described the weeks leading up to Oct. 27 as a particularly sensitive period and held a joint assessment this week focused on ensuring the election can be held safely. The warning comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that Washington would not attack Iran “at any time prior to the midterm elections” on November 3. Trump said talks with Tehran were “productive,” while insisting that the pressure campaign and blockade against Iran would remain in force. Despite Trump’s declaration, the IDF remains on heightened alert. The Israeli Air Force and Military Intelligence Directorate are maintaining readiness for a possible escalation with Iran, which the military continues to regard as its primary strategic theater. Any Israeli involvement in another major confrontation with Tehran would be coordinated with Washington. The IDF and U.S. military have remained in close coordination since the end of the latest round of fighting with Iran. Israeli military intelligence is meanwhile building an extensive new target bank inside Iran, covering ballistic missiles, launch and production infrastructure and sites connected to Tehran’s nuclear program. The IDF declined to comment on Zamir’s reported remarks. The warning fits a broader pattern of heightened preparations ahead of the election. Zamir recently canceled a planned trip to the United States, where he had been due to meet the commander of U.S. Central Command and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, saying the security situation made it inappropriate for him to leave Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also warned during a visit to Tel Nof Air Base last week that there were “signs” Israel’s enemies could attempt an attack ahead of the election. “Don’t mess with us, not now and not ever,” he said. “Our long arm will reach you anywhere and at any time.”
news.summary: Zamir raised the scenario in talks with senior US officials as the IDF keeps the Israel Air Force and Military Intelligence on heightened readiness and builds new target lists in Iran; Trump says Washington will not strike Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections
news.author: Elisha Ben Kimon

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed responds to President Trump's Truth Social attack
news.text:
Michigan Senate Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed snapped back at President Donald Trump's late-night Islamophobic Truth Social tirade, where he repeatedly called him "Mohammed" and a "terrorist sympathizer."

The night before the first Senate debate between El-Sayed and Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Rogers, Trump on Oct. 7 also called El-Sayed "a RADICAL Extremist," adding that "Mohammed’s Values are not exactly those of Michiganders, or those of our Great United States of America!" The president reiterated his "TOTAL ENDORSEMENT" for Rogers.

El-Sayed, seeking to be the first Muslim U.S. senator, responded Oct. 8, saying Trump knows his "name is Abdul" and that the president says it daily.

"But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us," El-Sayed said about the president in a post on X. "He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better.

"It’s time for change," added El-Sayed, a former public health official who won a contentious Democratic Senate primary against Rep. Hayley Stevens in August to secure the Democratic nomination for Senate.

Trump's comments and El-Sayed's response come as many polls show a tight race between El-Sayed and Rogers, capturing national attention as the Senate election is critical to Democrats' quest to take control of the Senate. Their Oct. 8 debate arrives as more than 200,000 Michiganders have already cast absentee ballots.

Who is Abdul El-Sayed?: The physician's path to the Dems' Michigan Senate nomination

El-Sayed, Rogers finally scheduled for first debate

A day after winning the Democratic Senate primary, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, sent a message to Rogers, Trump and other Republicans during his victory speech ahead of possible attacks during the campaign trail.

"They think they want to use my whole name against me. Mike, listen, man, if you can’t say the name — it’s Abdulrahman — keep the name out of your damn mouth," El-Sayed said. "I’ll be happy to give you lessons." 

Also at that speech, El-Sayed challenged Rogers to five debates. Although Rogers skipped a Sept. 15 debate against El-Sayed in Detroit over moderator issues, the two candidates are scheduled to finally take the stage Oct. 8 in Grand Rapids for their first face-to-face encounter.

A progressive and self-proclaimed capitalist candidate endorsed by former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, El-Sayed has energized fellow progressives and young voters. However, El-Sayed has some moderate Democrats concerned about his views, his tense relations with local Jewish communities and his ability to win retiring Democrat Sen. Gary Peters' seat against Rogers.
news.author: Usa Today

news.title: The Pentagon Is Eating Silicon Valley
news.text:
Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War, by Sharon Weinberger, Little, Brown and Company, 320 pages, $32

Donald Trump reportedly consulted a chatbot before attacking Venezuela. After an artificial intelligence told him Venezuelans would celebrate the overthrow of their regime, the president came away from the operation "thinking Grok was ingenious," Time reports, based on conversations with Trump and his advisers.

A few months later, another AI nearly started another war. With the help of a chatbot, someone at U.S. Special Operations Command wrote a report about a Chinese ship bringing nuclear weapons parts to Iran. The U.S. military nearly attacked the vessel before realizing that the chatbot had steered the official wrong, according to CNN.

Killer robots have long been a part of the popular imagination, but fewer people predicted automated yes-men whispering in the ears of military leaders. Weirder yet, these yes-men are a consumer product that anyone can use. Grok had 117 million monthly users as of March 2026, according to SpaceX corporate filings, and what U.S. Special Operations Command has is "mostly just copies of the commercial stuff wearing lipstick," an official told CNN. Last year, the U.S. military signed $200 million deals with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and xAI (owned by SpaceX) to integrate their systems with military databases.

"The most likely application of AI models" by the military is "identifying potential targets that could then be destroyed by weapons. In other words, the models, which are in some cases trained and refined on data from people seeking information on everything from medical problems to marital issues, could now be applied to warfare," Sharon Weinberger writes in her new book, Valley of Death. It's akin to the dilemma Weinberger notes about Amazon providing cloud computing for the U.S. government: "A company that has years of data on your purchases of everything from books to medications also provides remote servers for intelligence agencies."

Weinberger, a journalist who has been covering the weapons industry for more than two decades, argues that commercial tech companies and the military-industrial complex have fundamentally transformed each other. Rather than publicly traded corporations specializing in weapons, Pentagon contracts now go to billionaires "straddling the commercial and federal marketplaces." Tech entrepreneurs shape their strategies around locking in taxpayer-funded contracts and state-enforced monopolies. Investors call themselves providers of "patriotic capital." Government agencies rush to invest in promising technologies. The products we use in everyday life are being shaped around military needs.

"Every drone company I had five years ago was a drone delivery company trying to sell to Walmart, and today they're military-first, and 90 percent of their revenue is from the military," venture capitalist Clayton Williams tells Weinberger. Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, who made virtual reality headsets for video games before moving into weapons development, predicts to Weinberger that "you are going to see augmented reality on every soldier's head before you see it on every consumer's head."

Silicon Valley has never been completely disconnected from state violence. The semiconductor manufacturers that put San Francisco at the frontier of electronics were largely providing parts for military equipment. Larry Ellison, the Oracle owner who recently refashioned himself as a media mogul, got into the I.T. business building a database for the CIA in the 1970s. And if there was a gap between the hippie hackers and the buttoned-down national security state, the CIA helped bridge it by bailing out Apple founder Steve Jobs. He advertised himself as fighting Big Brother and once stubbornly refused to "do business for the fucking federal government," but Jobs' company NeXT would have gone out of business in 1989 if the agency hadn't bought thousands of his computers, which private industry found expensive and not very useful.

The CIA used those computers for analyzing satellite imagery, using graphics technology developed by Pixar. Ten years later, the agency created a venture capital firm called In-Q-Tel to fund promising technological startups.

One of In-Q-Tel's earliest ventures was Palantir, a data processing company. Like Jobs, its founder Peter Thiel had a libertarian streak early on. Thiel told Wired in 2001 that his best-known company, PayPal, would foster "the ability to move money fluidly" and "the erosion of the nation-state." Less than two weeks after that magazine issue appeared, Al Qaeda attacked America and Thiel reinvented himself. "The secret coordination of the world's intelligence services," he wrote in 2007, would be "the decisive path to a truly global pax Americana."

A few years later, future OpenAI founder Sam Altman invited Thiel to give a guest lecture at a class Altman was teaching. "Competition is for losers," Thiel preached, telling the class that "you always want to aim for monopoly."

Although Thiel is aligned with the Republican Party, it was a Democratic administration that helped his vision take off. President Barack Obama began surging troops to Afghanistan in 2009, and Palantir promised to help stop the Afghan insurgency by integrating many different sources of surveillance data. (The technology was based on PayPal's fraud-detection techniques.) The company gave U.S. troops free access to its database software and even sent its engineers into the country in hopes of making Palantir indispensable to the war. Obama's surge failed to pacify Afghanistan, but Thiel's gambit succeeded at bringing him business.

Afghanistan also birthed an important part of the AI revolution: image recognition. The U.S. military began deploying Gorgon Stare, a drone-based camera system that could surveil an entire city at once, over Afghan territory. (According to Weinberger, Gorgon Stare was inspired by the 1998 movie Enemy of the State, about a rogue surveillance apparatus.) The system was simply capturing too much footage for human beings to watch, so the military began Project Maven, hiring civilian AI companies to develop better image recognition technology. When Google employees objected to participating, Palantir swooped in to take the contract. Project Maven became a comprehensive battlefield surveillance system, helping watch over the last U.S. troops leaving Afghanistan and contributing to the 2026 aerial massacre of schoolchildren in Minab, Iran.

The leading AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic, originally promised not to get into the business of killing people. Weinberger calls this "a distinction without a difference," because they don't exclude helping to draw lists of targets. In 2024, OpenAI announced a partnership with Anduril on target detection and Anthropic announced a partnership with Palantir on "classified environments." As Weinberger points out, these could turn people's innocent queries into training data for killer robots.

Valley of Death hints at a big contradiction between how tech moguls speak and what they actually do. It's almost a dogma in the tech industry that the U.S. needs to be ready for war with China by 2027. Yet Silicon Valley's comfort zone is clearly with counterinsurgencies, not conflicts between great powers. Its technologies are better suited to imposing control from above than fighting a peer on equal ground.

The Russian invasion of Ukraine was a dry run for great power conflict. Although American military tech executives tried to make a big show of their contribution to the Ukrainian war effort, products from Palantir and Anduril proved mediocre compared to homegrown Ukrainian systems. "It's almost impossible to develop something that works without the contact with the problem space," Ukrainian technologist Andrey Liscovich told Weinberger, arguing that American technology companies lose their nimbleness in his country. And the challenge facing Ukraine is not really about making weapons smarter; it's about producing them cheaply at scale. In other words, great power conflict is an issue of physical bottlenecks, not intelligence.

The industry's enthusiastic engagement with Israel after October 7, 2023, which Weinberger portrays as a deviation from its otherwise China-focused strategy, makes more sense as a reversion to the mean. The U.S. focus turned back to fighting low-tech guerrillas and managing unruly populations. That was Silicon Valley's comfort zone. While insisting that China is still his No. 1 priority, Anduril's Luckey pitches Weinberger on a technology for dealing with tunnels in Gaza. He slips in the possibility that competition with China tomorrow will involve proxy wars like those of today. Of course.

In the war with Iran, "there is still little to show of startup technologies being used" by the U.S. military, Weinberger notes. (The two notable exceptions are Palantir's Maven database and SpaceX's satellite communications.) And that may serve Silicon Valley just fine. With so much military spending focused on capturing tomorrow's technologies, startup aerospace contractors can still "get to billions of dollars of revenue without an aircraft that flies," a venture capitalist brags to Weinberger. "Silicon Valley's 'fake it till you make it' works until people die," former CIA officer James Acuna tells her. That isn't a problem for most of the industry, yet.

Weinberger wonders whether putting power in the hands of private businessmen is dangerous for democracy. A better question may be whether it's good for the private marketplace. Increasingly insulated from the need to make money from customers, Silicon Valley has moved from technologies that enhance life and freedom to technologies that seek to destroy both.
news.summary: An influx of military spending has been moving tech companies away from serving consumers and back toward chasing government contracts.
news.author: Matthew Petti

news.title: Who Is Natalie Harp? All About Trump's Very Young Blonde Aide, 35, Amid Concerns Over Their 'Unhealthy Bond'
news.text:
Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old White House aide to President Donald Trump, is in the national spotlight after Sen. Jon Ossoff mentioned her by name in a speech criticizing the president.

"He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar," the Georgia Democrat said. 

The White House pushed back hard. 

"Jon Ossoff is a cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid," Spokesman Davis Ingle described Harp as “one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team.”

RadarOnline.com can reveal all you need to know about Harp.Natalie Harp Grew Up in California and Says She Battled Bone CancerHarp grew up in California, according to a publication. She has said she had bone cancer and credits a bill Trump signed in 2018 with giving her access to experimental treatments.Natalie Harp Caught Trump's Attention on Fox News in 2019She was telling that story on Fox News in 2019 when Trump took notice. He later invited her to speak at the 2020 Republican National Convention. 

Harp went on to anchor at One America News Network before joining his team in 2022.Natalie Harp Is Known as Trump's 'Human Printer'Today, Harp is a special assistant and executive assistant to the president, and reportedly earns a $150,000 salary.

She is also nicknamed the "human printer" because she carries a portable printer so she can hand Trump articles and other material on paper. 

Sources claimed the aide also passes along messages from allies, sets up meetings, and taps out Truth Social posts.Natalie Harp's Closeness to Trump Has Reportedly Raised EyebrowsHer devotion has raised eyebrows inside the White House. Two sources told CNN that in October 2023, Harp jumped into an SUV trunk after staffers said there was no room for her in the motorcade headed to a New York courthouse. 

It was also reported that her presence has irked some senior aides. One source claimed she has told others she reports only to Trump. A White House official downplayed those complaints and said she works well with most colleagues.

Harp also wrote two separate letters to Trump.

“I want things to always be right between us. I also know I’ve been distracted all week (forgetting to eat throughout the days, and even forgetting to sleep, and only catching a couple hours at a time)," one letter reads. 

The letter concludes: “With all my heart, Natalie.”

One person familiar with the situation claimed that Harp and Trump have a "father-daughter" relationship.
news.summary: Natalie Harp, 35, is in the spotlight after Sen. Jon Ossoff named her in a speech. Here's what to know about Trump's close aide
news.author: Sanu Abraham

news.title: 'I Can Do Whatever I Want': Trump Claims He Could Have Done 'Bad Things' to Former Prez's Biden and Obama
news.text:
Donald Trump has sparked a fresh firestorm with another eyebrow-raising, off-the-cuff remark, boasting he can "do whatever I want" when it comes to going after his Democratic adversaries, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

The president, 80, name dropped his predecessors Joe Biden and Barack Obama, as well as his 2016 challenger Hillary Clinton, boasting that he could have unleashed "very bad things" on the trio.'I Could Have Done Very Bad Things' to Democrat PredecessorsWhile Trump sat behind the Oval Office's Resolute Desk taking questions from reporters on Wednesday, October 7, one shouted out, "You've started telling midterm voters, if the Democrats win control of Congress, they will impeach you. For what?"

The Commander-in-Chief responded by claiming he saw three different Democrat lawmakers being asked the question about what they would impeach him for, "and they didn't know...one of them was just dumbfounded by the question."

Trump then made the highly provocative claim, "With that being said, I could have done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could have done very very bad things to Joe Biden. I could have done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama."

However, he noted, "I thought it was inappropriate to do so because you have to treat the office of the presidency with respect."Trump Claims 'I Can Do Whatever I Want'The reporters seemingly wanted to see where Trump was going with his statement as he went on to claim, "They impeached me twice. And to this moment, I can do whatever I want if I want. They've done some very bad things, many illegal things."

The tycoon reiterated, "But I view the presidency as a very sacred position...a position where it has to be treated publicly."

Trump went on to gripe about how the word "impeachment" was a "very seldom used word" in politics. Hillary's husband, Bill Clinton, was the first modern-era president to get impeached over allegedly lying to Congress about an affair with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. He was acquitted in1999. 

Trump made history as the first U.S. president to be impeached twice, first in 2019 on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, and again in 2021 for incitement of insurrection following the deadly January 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol. He was acquitted by the Senate both times.'I've Had Plenty of People Say Let's Go Get' Democrat Foes"They went after me twice. I won overwhelmingly. Both of them were thrown out overwhelimingly, I was never even worried about it," Trump sneered about his two impeachments. 

He contined, "You can't treat the presidency with disrespect. And again, I've had my shot and still do. I've had plenty of people say let's go get them," referring to Clinton, Biden and Obama. "And I said, 'No you can't do that to the presidency."Trump's Foes Claim His Comments Are 'Words of a Dictator'Trump's latest controversial remark came hot on the heels of another firestorm sparked at a Nebraska campaign rally, where he joked that a nuclear-armed Iran could "take out Los Angeles" or "take out San Diego" – two reliably Democratic California cities – triggering a fresh wave of outrage.

"He casually offered up two of our largest cities for annihilation by the enemy because they're located in a state that doesn't support him. Now he threatens opposition leaders and claims 'I can do whatever I want.' THIS IS UN-AMERICAN AND AUTHORITARIAN AND FRANKLY TREASONOUS," one person fumed on X. 

A second person huffed, "Firstly, he wants Iran to 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego, and now this. The words of a dictator," while a third sighed, "Someone make him stop talking; it's repulsive."
news.summary: Donald Trump made the rant after being asked if he'll likely get impeached if the Democrats take back Congress in the midterm election.
news.author: Beth Shilliday

news.title: Long-deployed US aircraft carrier returns home after 265 days at sea
news.text:
Mr Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.

The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.

Families and loved ones of the crew arrived hours ahead of the carrier’s arrival on Thursday, waiting in line to get on the naval base in Coronado near San Diego.

Among the first to depart once the ship docks will be 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said.

Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her six-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.

“She’s our deployment baby,” said Ms Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.

“We are different people now; we are parents now,” she said. “We definitely matured from the last time we saw each other.”

It was tough to hear about the ship’s conditions while she was pregnant, she said. “I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn’t sure if he was OK or not,” she said.

When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was “pretty bad”.

Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas, to name a few.

He had told his wife about “the lack of food and showers” on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned four while he was away, she said.

The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough”.

Mr Hegseth told the crew that “what makes the US military and the US Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless”.

The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January.

US and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on February 28.

Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time.

He said in a letter to a Democratic official seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln’s crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy said that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

According to the citation that Mr Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

The Lincoln played a vital role providing security for maritime operations in the Middle East, the Navy said.

The Lincoln, which set a record for days between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterwards.

In May, Mr Hegseth met the crew of the USS Gerald R Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

The deployment didn’t include as many uninterrupted days at sea as the Lincoln’s 265-day stretch.

Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.
news.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Bay after a record-long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of ...

news.title: 'He's not a p***y President': Mike Tyson launches wild defense of Trump and says president has overcome problems only 'black' people face
news.text:
Donald Trump is 'not a p***y President,' according to his longtime friend and boxing legend Mike Tyson. 

Speaking on the latest episode of Piers Morgan Uncensored, Tyson discussed his history with Trump, whom he first met as a young heavyweight in the 1980s as the future President was making a name for himself in New York and Atlantic City real estate. 

'I voted for him,' the 60-year-old Tyson told Morgan. 'I ran the streets for him. You know, me getting votes… I'm very proud of him. He's somebody that everybody should be proud of.' 

Tyson doesn't have many remaining personal ties to his early days in the ring. The boxing legend's famed trainer, Cus D'Amato, died in 1985, his turbulent marriage to actress Robin Givens ended four years later and Tyson's fragile business relationship with promoter Don King finally ruptured in the late 1990s.

But for all of the turnover surrounding Tyson, Trump has been a constant for the former heavyweight champion. Not only did Tyson fight at Trump's hotels and casinos, later adding the real estate mogul to his unofficial entourage, but the two remained friends throughout the ups and downs of their later lives. 

And it's those obstacles that make Trump an admirable figure in the eyes of Tyson: 'Listen, if you didn't know who Donald Trump was and you didn't know his name, you would think he's Black.'

According to Tyson, it's Trump's perseverance in the face of multiple bankruptcies and sexual misconduct allegations that have made him a formidable figure. 

'When he went for President, he was bankrupt... He owed taxes, he owed so much money,' Tyson said, somewhat erroneously. 

While Trump's businesses did declare bankruptcy six times, the last filing came in 2009, well before his successful 2016 White House run.

But it's not just the financial problems that give Trump credibility in Tyson's eyes. Tyson was also impressed with the way Trump survived multiple waves of sexual misconduct claims. 

'All this sex abuse and all that stuff that he went through,' Tyson continued. 'People don't normally go that well. They normally have a nervous breakdown. He handled it. And that's why everyone has to respect him. Just from the way he handled his court procedures… I don't care if you hate his guts… you have to respect that. Just off the bat.'

Trump has never been convicted of any sexual misconduct, although in May of 2023, a federal jury found him liable in a civil trial for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll. A later trial resulted in a federal jury ordering Trump to pay an additional $83.3 million on top of the initial $5 million penalty he was ordered to pay Carroll.

Previously, Trump supported Tyson in the face of sexual misconduct claims. When Tyson was convicted of rape in Indiana in 1992, the future President told NBC the boxer was 'railroaded in the case' and questioned the victim's story.

Trump went so far as to publicly suggest Tyson should be allowed to dodge prison by giving 'millions and millions' of dollars to the victim.

'What has happened to him, the conviction, is already punitive,' Trump told the New York Post in 1992. 'The victim has had the satisfaction of humbling him and being vindicated.'

Speaking with Morgan, Tyson did not address the support he received from Trump in 1992.

He did, however, discuss the assassination attempt Trump survived in Pennsylvania on the campaign trail in 2024 by explaining he is 'not a p**** President.' 

As for his immediate future, Tyson's planned exhibition with Floyd Mayweather Jr. is currently on hold after the former heavyweight broke his hand in May. Another complicating factor is a lawsuit against Mayweather by the promoter, CSI Sports.

In his previous return to the ring in 2024, Tyson was easily defeated by cruiserweight Jake Paul, who scored a unanimous decision victory that was watched by an estimated 60 million households on Netflix.
news.summary: Speaking on the latest episode of Piers Morgan Uncensored, Tyson discussed his history with Trump, whom he first met as a young heavyweight in the 1980s.

news.title: More than half of Canadians are avoiding buying American goods, poll finds
news.text:
More than half of Canadians are actively avoiding American products as ongoing trade disputes and import bans continue to reshape cross-border shopping habits, according to new national survey data from Abacus Data. 

The September poll found that 51 percent of Canadian shoppers avoid U.S. goods when possible. That figure is up from 38 percent recorded in February 2025, when initial U.S. tariff threats first emerged.

Broader tracking by Abacus Data shows that 77 percent of Canadians currently intend to buy as few American products as possible or avoid them entirely, a level of consumer resistance that has held steady over the past 19 months.

The Canadian consumer pushback follows deepening trade friction between Washington and Ottawa. The U.S. recently enacted an import ban targeting roughly $1 billion in Canadian goods, including dairy items, motorcycles and alcoholic beverages. The move came in response to 50 percent tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump earlier this summer, which led Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to hit back with matching counter-tariffs.

“There is now a price to be paid for access to the United States market,” Carney stated, outlining a broader target to double non-U.S. commerce within ten years while seeking deeper trade links with the European Union, India and China.

The trade measures are also affecting American consumers. An upcoming U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule suspending the $800 duty-free de minimis exemption threatens to disrupt how an estimated 2.3 million Americans buy lower-cost prescription drugs through Canadian pharmacies. 

Critics and patients warn that added fees, bond requirements and existing tariffs will push prices up on vital medications.

“The issue is a matter of life and death for me,” said Susan Hooper, a 75-year-old Ohio resident who relies on imported Canadian prescriptions for asthma and airway management. Hooper said that tariffs have already pushed her monthly cost for one medication from $85 to $141.

For Canadian grocery retailers, the shift in domestic consumer sentiment is driving operational demands. Seven in 10 survey respondents want stores to remove American goods from their shelves entirely. In contrast, 89 percent want clear labeling on domestic items, and 87 percent want grocers to expand their stock of Canadian and non-U.S. alternatives.

However, price and brand recognition remain hurdles for domestic shoppers. According to Abacus Data, 61 percent of Canadians still assume that domestic alternatives cost more than similar American items, and fewer than half can reliably identify whether specific brands on supermarket shelves are Canadian-owned.

This shift in consumer behavior isn't isolated to Canada. 

A separate international study by Bloomberg and Morning Consult revealed that consumers across 13 European and Asian countries are spending less on U.S. brands compared to five years ago, Retail Brew reported. Malaysia recorded the highest drop, with 55 percent of consumers reducing their spending on U.S. goods, followed by France at 47 percent, China at 46 percent, South Korea at 43 percent and Singapore at 42 percent.

American fast food and coffee chains have experienced the largest drops in global spending.

Sixty percent of respondents in the U.K., China and Indonesia said they had cut back spending in those sectors, with similar declines reported in Germany at 59 percent and France at 57 percent.

According to data reported by Bloomberg and Morning Consult, a shift in U.S. political leadership or strategic direction would have the highest effect in reversing those habits in Germany, where 56 percent of consumers said a political change would encourage them to resume buying U.S. brands, followed by 47 percent in the U.K.
news.summary: Canadian shoppers are pressuring grocery stores to respond, with nearly nine in 10 wanting clear labels on domestic products
news.author: Jasmine Fernández

news.title: USS Abraham Lincoln's Condition As It Makes Port: What Photos Show
news.text: The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived at its home port of San Diego on Thursday, with those waiting on the shore getting a first glimpse of the ship that spent 10 months on deployment. The carrier’s record-setting period of consecutive days at sea was dogged with reports of law morale, suicide attempts and lack of food. It also drew scrutiny last month, when it was pictured with rust and algae on its hull, with paint missing from its waterline, while it made port in Laem Chabang, on the Gulf of Thailand, south of Bangkok. Families and locals gathered to see the ship arrive back on the California coast, with banners and flags greeting those on board. The Lincoln Returns Home Ahead of the Lincoln's arrival, national and state officials shared messages to the crew on social media, including former Vice President Mike Pence. "Your Safe Return is Answered Prayer," he wrote on X. "Congratulations on a Job Well Done in Operation Epic Fury! America is Proud of You All!" San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said he hoped the days ahead brought rest, healing and joy to those on board. "For more than 300 days, these service members were separated from their families and the community they call home. They answered every call placed before them with courage, professionalism and extraordinary resilience," Gloria said in a statement shared to X. "This homecoming also belongs to their families. They endured months of uncertainty, missed milestones and long stretches with limited communication while continuing to support their loved ones from thousands of miles away. We know this deployment took a serious toll. As these men and women return, they deserve the time, care and resources necessary to rest, recover and reconnect with the people they love." Hegseth's Message to the Crew Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited the crew on board on Wednesday, ahead of its official return after 321 days at sea, when the crew went 264 days without a port call. President Donald Trump “wanted me to personally thank you, each and every one of you, from the Oval Office for what you have done here,” Hegseth told the crew. But the ship underwent some cleaning when during its Thailand port visit, leaving its exterior fresher for its homecoming. On Wednesday, Hegseth spoke out against “a few folks in the media” whom he said tried to turn the Lincoln’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.” Newsweek has contacted the U.S. Navy via email for comment. Lincoln's Deployment The Lincoln was part of America’s “Operation Epic Fury” in Iran from February through August, when it carried out 40 days of combat operations in the monthslong blockade of Iran in and around the Strait of Hormuz. "We landed on the most beautiful of days, in the middle of an empty flight deck because [the air wing] is gone, and [you were] landing in the middle of the night in dangerous territory with a full flight deck during combat operations, and you didn't miss a beat," Hegseth told the crew. The crew sank 64 Iranian warships, Hegseth said, carried out 3,693 combat sorties (individual flights on combat missions), launching 450 Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles (long-range missiles launched from ships to hit targets on land), shot down 77 drones and defended itself against missiles and boats. Scrutiny Over Lincoln’s Appearance At the beginning of September, images showed rust and worn-off paint on the exterior of the carrier. Experts told Newsweek at the time that this was to be expected as part of the wear and tear a ship goes through during deployment. The condition of the Lincoln's hull and paint missing from the waterline is "consistent" with more than nine months at sea and is "cosmetic," rather than impacting how the carrier operates, said retired U.S. Navy Vice Admiral Robert Murrett, who is now a professor of practice of public administration and international affairs at Syracuse University. Similarly, William Freer, a research fellow in national security at the U.K.-based Council on Geostrategy think tank, said: "Though the wear and tear looks extensive, that a ship commissioned in 1989 was able to operate for such a prolonged period of time without facing issues is testament to the U.S. Navy's ability to put ships through their operational paces when the need arises." The ship was cleaned in Thailand, with multiple defense accounts on X previously sharing footage of workers hosing down the vessel's hull. Reports of Suicide Attempts and Food Shortages In August, the U.S. Navy denied claims of attempted suicides on board the aircraft carrier, after family members of the crew reportedly raised welfare concerns. Military publication the Navy Times reported that at least two U.S. Navy sailors had attempted to jump overboard from the vessel, citing relatives. The Pentagon later told Newsweek: "Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship," a spokesperson said. "We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise." A few months earlier, reports emerged about food shortages on the ship, which the Pentagon denied. Gerald D. Givens Jr., a retired member of the U.S. Air Force and the founder and CEO of Raleigh Boots on the Ground, a nonprofit that supports military families, said in April that he received photos showing this from a friend whose son was serving on the ship. Photos showed trays containing what appear to be minimal portions of food, including a single meat patty, a small serving of shredded meat and sparse side items. "[My friend] told me her son has lost 17 pounds," Givens told Newsweek. "Her husband, also a close friend and a retired veteran, shared that a care package they sent in December still has not arrived." The Pentagon denied any suggestions of food shortages on board ships and did not comment on the pictures. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Rebecca Flood and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln has docked back home in California, looking cleaner and fresher than when it made port in Thailand.
news.author: Dan Gooding,Jordan King

news.title: CNN Data Guru Says Key Group Has Turned on Trump
news.text:
President Donald Trump is “underwater” with millennials, according to CNN’s chief data analyst Harry Enten.

Trump was previously on “the plus side of the ledger” among voters aged 30 to 44, Enten said on CNN’s News Central on Thursday. But over the past year, his net approval rating has plummeted from +5 to -36. 

“He’s more underwater than the New York Yankees’ favorability in the Bronx right now,” Enten quipped.

Enten said the shift is because of the economy, which Trump is getting “absolutely crushed” on. 

In 2024, he had a net approval rating of +36 for his handling of the economy. Now, that number has fallen to -37. 

“The reason he did so well with millennials back in 2024 was because they looked back at the economy during the Trump years and gave it two thumbs up,” Enten said. “But now the Siskel and Ebert is two thumbs down, moving away from the president of the United States on the key issue of the day, the economy.”

The data also shows millennials favoring the Democrats by 22 points. 

“This idea that millennials are moving into the Republican camp, they may have been back in 2024, but if you look at it right now in 2026, they are returning to the Democratic fold,” Enten said.

The polling looks grim for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms, with Democrats currently leading in several key races. 

And, according to a new Gallup poll on party affiliation, more Americans identify as Democrats than at any point since 2009.

The president is currently touring deep-red and Republican-leaning states to shore up his base ahead of the midterms. 

But a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that, among voters enthusiastic about November’s elections, opposition to Trump is a more powerful motivator than support for him. 

Sixty-two percent said they were excited to vote against him, compared to 36 percent who said they were eager to support him.
news.summary:
REUTERS/Evan VucciPresident Donald Trump is “underwater” with millennials, according to CNN’s chief data analyst Harry Enten.

Trump was previously on “the plus side of the ledger” among voters aged 30 to 44, Enten said on CNN’s News Central on Thursday. But over the past year, his net approval rating has plummeted from +5 to -36.
