news.title: Pope Leo's Chances Of Winning Nobel Peace Prize
news.text: With the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize set to be announced on Friday, Newsweek has looked at the market odds of Pope Leo XIV winning. The pontiff has made world peace a central theme of his papacy, repeatedly calling for the end to wars around the world, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the war in the Middle East. He has offered the Vatican as a venue for negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv, urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to pursue a ceasefire in Gaza and has been critical of U.S. President Donald Trump’s war in Iran. It is not known whether Pope Leo is an official nominee, as the Nobel Committee keeps nominations confidential for 50 years, but his name is featured in major market odd platforms. Both Polymarket and Kalshi show Leo’s odds at 2 percent, as of Thursday morning, on par with Doctors Without Borders and the International Criminal Court. How Pope Leo’s Chances Compare With Other Candidates Pope Leo is priced above Trump (1 percent) on both platforms, where Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms lead with 17 percent on Polymarket and 16 percent on Kalshi. The organization is a network providing humanitarian aid to people affected by the country’s civil war. Polymarket lists other likely candidates as Ukrainian children’s rights advocate Mykola Kuleba (9 percent), Save the Children (8 percent) and Yulia Navalnaya (5 percent), a Russian opposition activist and the widow of Alexei Navalny. Kalshi gives Kuleba 10 percent odds. Other possibilities include the International Criminal Court of Justice, the Committee to Protect Journalists and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. What Pope Leo XIV has Done To Promote Peace Leo used his first Sunday Regina Caeli, in May 2025, to appeal to world leaders to work against war. “I carry in my heart the sufferings of the beloved Ukrainian people. May everything possible be done to reach an authentic, just and lasting peace, as soon as possible,” he said. “Let all the prisoners be freed and the children return to their own families.” Leo then said: “I am deeply saddened by what is happening in the Gaza Strip: may there be an immediate ceasefire! Let humanitarian aid be provided to the stricken civil population, and let all the hostages be freed.” A month later, Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin about Ukraine, humanitarian aid and prisoner exchanges. “The Pope made an appeal for Russia to make a gesture that would favour peace,” a Holy See Press Office statement said. Leo then met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, offering the Vatican as a venue for negotiations. He spoke with Netanyahu in July, met with Zelensky again in July and, just last week, joined hundreds of children in praying the rosary for peace. Leo’s Feud With Trump Over Iran War Earlier this year, Leo strongly condemned the war in the Middle East, and the "delusion of omnipotence" that caused it, saying it has led to "absurd and inhuman violence." In April, when Trump wrote on social media that "an entire civilization will die tonight" if Iran failed to meet a U.S. deadline, Leo responded: "This is truly unacceptable." Trump later posted a scathing attack on the pope in a post on Truth Social, calling him "weak on crime" and "terrible for foreign policy." When Trump accused Leo of “rather talk [ing]about the fact that it's OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” Leo said: "If anyone wishes to criticize me for proclaiming the Gospel, let them do so with the truth. The Church has spoken out for years against all nuclear weapons, so there is no doubt about this, and I simply hope to be heard for the sake of the Word of God." Leo and Trump administration officials have downplayed the rift. Leo previously said there has been a "narrative that has not been accurate in all of its aspects." Has Any Pope Won A Peace Prize? No pope has ever won the Nobel Peace Prize, but the following have been nominated, according to official nomination records. Former Pope Benedict XV was nominated in 1915, 1916 and 1920, according to official nomination records, and former Pope Paul VI was nominated in 1967 and 1972. news.summary: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize set to be announced on Friday.

news.title: Jon Stewart tells Democrats to 'govern' and skip 'performative' Trump impeachment if they win
news.text: Comedian Jon Stewart urged Democrats not to pursue impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump if they regain control of the House and Senate, arguing on his podcast that he doesn't want to see "performative" hearings. During a question-and-answer segment at the end of Stewart's "The Weekly Show" podcast, he was asked whether Democrats should seek to impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress in the midterm elections. He said he wanted to see Democrats make a full-scale effort to rebalance the economy, and said he didn't want to see performative hearings. "I don't want to see a f---ing five-act performative play of House hearings," Stewart said. "I just don't want to see it. I don't want to see everybody having the opportunity to pantomime accountability because you know they're actually not going to bring it." STEWART EXPECTS SCHUMER, JEFFRIES TO DISAPPOINT IF THE DEMS WIN BACK THE HOUSE AND SENATE "You want to do some investigations of some s---, that's great," he continued. "But on the triage list of what's wrong in this country, it is, 'I'm sorry, sir, you're going to have to stay in the waiting room because this guy just got shot, and it sounds to me like you just have a sore throat.' Like do the s--- that actually is killing people right now." Stewart added that he wanted Democrats to "govern." "You want to do some things that are ancillary, a little side project, you want to do the investigations as a hobby, knock yourself out. Fix s---," he said. "Jon Stewart is tapping into a real tension within the Democratic electorate," Lauryn Killian, CEO of Killian Campaigns, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "There will certainly be Democrats who want impeachment, particularly those who believe the Trump administration warrants aggressive congressional scrutiny." "But there is a meaningful difference between legitimate accountability and turning impeachment into another chapter of the anti-Trump resistance movement," she continued. "If Democrats take back Congress, voters will expect them to actually govern, not spend two years trying to undo the last election." HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY Killian said the smarter political strategy would be to look into "wrongdoing and pursue accountability where the facts warrant it, while focusing congressional energy on issues that actually affect Americans' lives: the economy, affordability, public safety and government competence." "Winning Congress would give Democrats an opportunity to demonstrate they can govern beyond simply being the opposition," she added. "If they turn that opportunity into another impeachment crusade, Republicans will have a very clear argument to make to voters: Democrats were given power to govern, and chose instead to keep fighting the last election." "Jon Stewart is saying what Democrats don't want to hear: voters want results, not revenge," Y. David Scharf, chair of government strategies and controversies at Morrison Cohen, told Fox News Digital. "If Democrats win Congress and spend the next two years trying to impeach Trump instead of lowering costs and fixing the economy, they'll be writing the Republican playbook for 2028." He described impeachment as "political theater." Democratic strategist James Carville and his podcast co-host Al Hunt also warned against impeachment on Tuesday. Carville and Hunt argued that impeachment would be a waste of time and Democrats should devote their energy to investigating the president instead. CARVILLE SAYS THE GOP IS BETTER THAN DEMOCRATS AT ONE KEY SKILL THE 2028 DEM NOMINEE WILL NEED "I’ll tell you one thing that I think Democrats should steer clear of, and that’s impeachment," Hunt said. "It’s not that Trump has not committed impeachable offenses, far worse than what he was accused of back in 2019 with Ukraine. I mean, he has. I mean, you could come up with a bill of particulars of, you know, a dozen at least. But you know something, James? It’s not going to happen, and it is a distraction." "It is a waste of energy," Hunt added. "Investigate, investigate, investigate. Don’t go on a mission that isn’t going to succeed." Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who also served as White House chief of staff, urged fellow Democrats not to pursue impeachment during an interview on Sunday. "You’re never going to get an impeachment," he said. "Then, if you do that, you just basically prove all [of] Washington is what the American people think. It’s Disneyland on the Potomac. Deliver the change. Deliver a comprehensive ethics package that uses the investigations to then deliver change." The warnings came as Democrats held a polling advantage over Republicans heading into the final weeks before the midterm elections. FORMER CHICAGO MAYOR RAHM EMANUEL DECLARES AMERICA IS READY FOR A JEWISH PRESIDENT House race projections show Democrats winning 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning Democrats would need to win at least three of the 19 remaining toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has declined to say whether he would support impeachment proceedings against Trump, though he appeared to suggest over the summer that impeachment would not be a top priority. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Anders Hagstrom and Alexander Hall contributed to this report.
news.summary: Jon Stewart warned Democrats against the "performative play" of impeaching President Donald Trump, urging the party to govern and fix the issues killing people now.

news.title: Fox News Insiders Reveal Truth About Network’s Trump Snubs
news.text:
Fox News is skipping Donald Trump’s midterm rallies because viewers are just not that into him anymore, network insiders have revealed. 

“This is coming from the top down,” a current Fox host told CNN, on condition of anonymity. “Trump doesn’t rate anymore.”

The traditionally Trump-friendly network’s shift comes as some Republican candidates are also distancing themselves from Trump ahead of the midterm elections.

“We talk so much about how Trump is the ‘executive producer in chief’ but often forget that even the most popular shows tend to run out of steam after one season too many,” veteran Republican strategist Doug Heye said.

“That’s exactly where we are and why — whether you’re in Lake of the Ozarks or Emmetsburg, Iowa, fewer Trump flags are being flown every day.”

Fox News, America’s most-watched cable channel, has historically been a major way for Trump to reach voters. But the network has hardly covered five of his rallies this week.

The 80-year-old president has melted down over his loss of coverage, calling the rallies “the hottest things out there” and complaining that “nothing shows up on Fox!”

“Sad to see that Fox & Friends (Sunday) is not covering our packed house and incredibly enthusiastic (beyond!) Rally that took place in Ohio last night, or the ones in Alabama, Texas, or Oklahoma over the past two days,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

Insiders are delivering a reality check, however. Trump “needs Fox way more than Fox needs him,” Mediaite co-managing editor and former Fox News staffer Tom Durante wrote on Wednesday.

Other conservative networks are hoping to capitalize on Fox’s limited coverage of Trump’s rallies.

Charles Herring, president of One America News, said his channel is running all of Trump’s midterm rallies, “generally commercial-free, typical of our live coverage of events.” 

But OAN’s viewership is significantly smaller than Fox’s. 

Laura Ingraham cut to Trump’s San Antonio, Texas, rally on her Wednesday show, but it was not the glorifying coverage Trump is used to getting from the network.

Correspondent Brooke Taylor gave the scene a harsh assessment. 

“This is a state he won by nearly 14 points just two years ago, and now he’s finding himself back here in Texas defending this state and keeping it red. I mean, hard to believe those words are even coming out of my mouth, right?”

Ingraham then turned to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent for an interview. 

At the end of the day, Fox News is a media company that needs to draw viewers in. 

In Durante’s words, “They [Fox] were around long before Trump became a political candidate. And they’ll be there long after he’s out of office.”

“This is coming from the top down,” a current Fox host told CNN, on condition of anonymity. “Trump doesn’t rate anymore.”

news.title: US freezes green-card processing for Microsoft, Adobe workers
news.text:
The United States government has suspended the processing of employment-based green-card applications involving major technology companies, including Microsoft and Adobe, over alleged abuse of the country’s skilled-worker immigration system, Reuters reports on Thursday.

The move, which also affects major information technology companies such as Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, is part of the Trump administration’s wider crackdown on employment-based immigration.

According to Reuters, the US Labour Department will stop accepting new applications and processing pending applications for permanent labour certification involving the named companies.

The certification, known as PERM, is required for many employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residence in the US.

Employers must generally demonstrate that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of American workers.

US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the system more than any other US company, pointing to layoffs at the technology giant while it continued to use the H-1B visa programme and seek green cards for foreign workers.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at a press conference on Thursday.

He stated, “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.

“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

Reuters reports that Microsoft disputed the suggestion that it was using the programme to replace American workers, saying about 80 per cent of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were for existing employees seeking extensions or changes of status rather than new hires.

The company also said H-1B workers were paid the same as comparable employees.

The Labour Secretary, Keith Sonderling, said the suspension covered the eight named companies and would remain in place as the administration investigated their use of the permanent labour certification system.

“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.

The companies have collectively sought nearly three million foreign workers since 2009, with more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications, according to Labour Department data cited by Reuters.

The action comes weeks after the Trump administration introduced a $100,000 fee for new H-1B petitions involving workers hired from abroad.

The administration’s Project Firewall has also opened about 200 cases and imposed millions of dollars in penalties as it investigates alleged violations involving the hiring of foreign workers.

The administration has accused some employers of posting ineffective job advertisements and then claiming that qualified American workers could not be found, allowing them to hire foreign workers at lower wages.

The companies affected by the latest action have not been found guilty of those allegations.

The freeze is therefore focused on employment-based immigration and does not mean that existing green-card holders or all immigrants in the US have lost their status.

The administration has also opened investigations into nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, over alleged misuse of exchange-visitor visas.

Vance said the university investigations were aimed at examining whether foreign workers and students were being used to undercut American wages, while the administration is also investigating alleged foreign influence and visa abuses.

The latest actions are part of President Donald Trump’s broader immigration policy, which has placed greater pressure on US employers to hire American workers rather than rely on foreign labour.
news.summary:
The US government has suspended processing employment-based green-card applications for Microsoft, Adobe, and others over alleged immigration system abuse.

US brings torture charges against Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro and wife Cilia Flores

Maduro and Cilia Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges after they were snatched from Caracas by the US military in January.

7.46pm, 8 Oct 2026

Share options

THE UNITED STATES has filed new torture charges against ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, bolstering a mounting criminal case against the pair held in US custody.

Maduro and Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges after they were snatched from their Caracas compound in an extraordinary US military raid in January.

A new court filing shows both are now further charged with conspiracy to commit torture against victims, including US citizens, in Venezuelan detention – with prosecutors detailing alleged waterboardings, rapes and beatings.

Torture was allegedly used to “intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings.”

In a 2022 instance, Venezuelan authorities allegedly tortured an American who they accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.

“That torture included electric shock to arms, legs, and genitals; asphyxiation; beatings; deprivation of food and water; and forced injections of a substance that caused (the victim) to experience seizures,” the filing states.

During his 2013-2026 presidency, rights groups widely accused Maduro of using political repression to cling to power.

“These additional charges reflect the dedication of this Administration to delivering justice for the victims of torture, narcoterrorism, and organized crime,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said on X.

FBI director Kash Patel said the latest charges showed Washington’s commitment to “accountability, the rule of law, and the protection of US national security.”

Advertisement

‘Prisoner of war’

Maduro and Flores are set to stand trial in New York next June and are being held in a Brooklyn jail.

US prosecutors claim that Maduro used state power to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling, and that he allied himself with cartels to ship tons of cocaine into the United States.

Maduro has denied the charges he originally faced: “narcoterrorism” conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices as well as conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

He has described himself as a “prisoner of war” and said the US military kidnapped him.

Flores has similarly pleaded not guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

She was charged today with “narcoterrorism” conspiracy, the court filing showed.

The pair have asked a US judge to dismiss the charges against them, claiming they have immunity as president and first lady of a sovereign country.

Since Maduro’s capture, vice president Delcy Rodriguez has governed Venezuela as interim leader under intense pressure from US president Donald Trump’s administration.

American energy firms have this year signed a raft of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela, which has agreed to grant the US control of a huge chunk of its vast oil reserves.

news.title: The Facebook whistleblower behind ‘The Social Reckoning’ says Zuckerberg is ‘playing with fire’ on AI
news.text:
The Facebook whistleblower on Meta’s AI bet.

OpenAI’s human rights lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night.’

Fired OpenAI safety staffers urge company to protect AI monitoring.

And voters increasingly see AI as a threat to American workers.

First, a quick note: Fortune Brainstorm AI returns to San Francisco Dec. 7–8 to convene technologists, entrepreneurs, Fortune Global 500 executives, investors, policymakers, and the brilliant minds in between to interrogate the most pressing questions about AI. We will explore how organizations are deploying and scaling AI in their industries. Come join me there. Apply to attend now

This week, director Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning, a follow-up to The Social Network, opens in U.S. cinemas. The 2010 film was about how Facebook was founded. This one is about the company’s moment of reckoning: whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision in 2021 to walk out of the company with tens of thousands of pages of internal documents.

Haugen, played by Mikey Madison in the new film, was a product manager on Facebook’s civic integrity team. She gave the documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, and they later became the basis of an investigative, award-winning series of stories that the Journal called The Facebook Files. Among other things, the series revealed that the company’s own researchers had found Instagram made body image issues worse for some teenage girls. Haugen filed whistleblower complaints with the SEC and testified before the Senate, and her disclosures have since helped drive a wave of lawsuits against social media companies.

I spoke with Haugen this week about how Facebook (now called Meta, of course) has changed since she walked out, what she makes of Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s AI push, and what she wants employees at the leading labs to take from the film.

“My hope for the movie is that people, especially at the frontier AI labs, see themselves in the Frances Haugen character. If they see something, feel like they can say something,” Haugen told Fortune.

But, in a moment where the AI industry is filled with existential anxiety, and even its leaders are calling for brakes, Haugen isn’t advocating for a pause in AI development.

“We have never done a prohibition where we could properly check,” she said. “Slowing down just means whoever doesn’t want to slow down wins.”

Instead, she’s backing a different part of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s recent plan: independent auditors. Amodei proposed that frontier labs give third-party evaluators ongoing, “employee-like access” to check safety practices and report incidents, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said his company would do the same. Haugen says the best mitigation to AI harms is for this kind of auditing to be required by law across the industry, the way outside auditors are entitled to review the books at banks.

AI companies already publish far more research into their products than Facebook ever did, she said, but she questions whether what they publish reflects what’s actually happening inside.

As for Meta, Haugen views Zuckerberg’s recent AI efforts as “playing with fire,” driven by his desire for a positive legacy. She also doesn’t think the company has changed since she blew the whistle. “I have not seen a culture change that shows that they have…turned a new leaf,” she said.

Meta is still behind leading labs like Anthropic and OpenAI—and Zuckerberg has been prominent in pushing back on regulatory efforts.

“He wants to catch up, so he wants there to be no constraints until he’s at least at the same table as the big boys,” she said of Zuckerberg’s anti-regulation stance, “not just pretending to be where the big boys are.”

(Fortune contacted Meta for comment on Haugen’s claims but the company did not reply before press time.)

AI content moderation

How Meta moderated harmful content on its platform was a big part of Haugen’s 2021 disclosures. Some of the internal documents she took suggested Facebook acted on as little as 3% to 5% of hate speech on the platform, and she has previously said the company’s decision to dissolve her civic integrity team after the 2020 election helped push her to come forward.

Last year, Meta shifted its automated content moderation toward high-severity violations and replaced some of its U.S. third-party fact-checking program with an X-style Community Notes system. This year it has gone further. In March, it said it would rely less on outside vendors and human contractors for enforcement, and in June the Financial Times reported that AI models had already taken over about half of human review requests.

Haugen expects better models to make fewer mistakes and catch more harmful content, but not all of it. When she left, the company was catching about 5% of harmful content, she said. But she predicts that even very advanced AI might only reach 10% to 20%, because language is so nuanced.

“The real solution is designing the systems from the ground up to be safer, not just trying to clean them up in the end,” she said.

With that, here’s more AI news.

Beatrice Nolanbeatrice.nolan@fortune.com@beafreyanolan

FORTUNE ON AI

OpenAI’s human rights lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’ — By Emily Forlini

OpenAI publishes solutions to more than 370 outstanding math challenges. The results divide mathematicians but most agree: Math will never be the same — By Jeremy Kahn 

IBM cyber response chief: After 26 years in incident response, I’m more concerned about burnout than AI — By Tony Kirtley 

AI IN THE NEWS

Fired OpenAI safety staffers urge company to protect AI monitoring. Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, who worked on OpenAI's safety and alignment teams, have written to the company's board and safety committees urging OpenAI to preserve its ability to monitor AI models' "chain of thought," a written record of how AI systems work through problems, and to collaborate with independent safety auditors, the Wall Street Journal reported. OpenAI said last week an internal investigation found the three had mishandled sensitive information outside established procedures, and reports linked the case to information shared with an outside AI safety organization. The new letter warns that the industry doesn't yet know how to safely build and deploy models whose reasoning process can't be monitored. It arrives as OpenAI's latest model, GPT-6 Astra, reportedly makes limited use of a more opaque form of reasoning called "recurrent depth," and after hundreds of OpenAI agents gained internet access in July and hacked Hugging Face without the company's knowledge. 

Isomorphic Labs in talks to raise at a $40 billion-plus valuation. Isomorphic Labs, the Alphabet company that uses AI to discover drugs, is in early talks to raise new funds at a valuation of at least $40 billion, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The round could value the Google DeepMind spinout at as much as $50 billion, though the financing hasn't closed and details could change. The talks come five months after the company closed a $2.1 billion Series B in May, led by Thrive Capital. That round's valuation was never disclosed, though outside estimates put it at roughly $10 billion to $20 billion. 

Fed officials say the data center boom is pushing prices higher. Federal Reserve officials are increasingly pointing to the AI buildout, rather than tariffs, to explain why the price of goods keeps rising, according to the Washington Post. Officials cited "surging AI-related investments" as a source of inflation pressure, alongside higher oil and fuel prices. Companies are borrowing heavily to fund the buildout of data centers and the purchase of chips and related hardware, and some officials warned it could push demand beyond what businesses can supply. A year ago, AI rarely came up in Fed discussions, the outlet said.

Meta deploys new AI tools to catch ads that funnel users to child abuse material. Meta said Wednesday it acted on 33.2 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content across Facebook and Instagram in the first half of 2026, and that its systems found more than 97% of it before any user reported it. The company is also rolling out new AI tools to counter a tactic it calls "signposting." These are ads that look harmless but steer users to illegal material hosted off Meta's platforms. A new LLM-based system checks where an ad sends users, not just what the ad contains, so Meta can block rule-breaking destinations and the accounts behind them. Meta is also deploying a red-teaming AI agent that probes its own safeguards for weaknesses bad actors could exploit. The tools arrive amid sustained pressure on the company over child safety. In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a lawsuit brought by 29 U.S. states. You can read more from TechCrunch here.

EYE ON AI NUMBERS

That's the share of American voters who see AI as a threat to workers, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll. That's more than say the same about competition from foreign workers or big corporations. Voters also don't think Washington is taking the risks seriously. More than half—57%—say the Trump administration hasn't taken AI risks seriously enough, including a third of Republicans. Support for tougher rules crosses party lines, with 80% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans backing stricter regulation.

The poll came out in the week after President Donald Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six leading AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. The companies agreed to work with independent auditors, but the deal sets no consequences for those that don't comply. You can read the full poll here.

AI CALENDAR

Nov. 16-17: Fortune 500 Innovation Forum, Detroit. Apply here to attend.

Dec. 6-12: Neural Information Processing Systems (Neurips) conference. Sydney, Australia.

Dec. 7-8: Fortune Brainstorm AI, San Francisco. Apply here to attend.
news.summary: The real Frances Haugen on the new Sorkin film, Meta’s AI spending spree, and why a pause won’t work.

news.title: Jared Kushner, 45, Drops Stunning Admission About His Education
news.text:
Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is furiously trying to push back on coverage of him, but in doing so, he made one glaring admission about his time at Harvard.

Kushner, 45, put up a lengthy post on Thursday taking aim at a profile of him in The New Yorker that was published last month titled “Jared Kushner’s Dollar Diplomacy.” 

The president’s son has been under the microscope for his work around the world for the Trump administration despite having no official government role and still conducting personal business.

In his latest attempt to “put the facts out there,” as he put it, Kushner shared a lengthy post disputing fourteen claims in the article. 

But among them, Kushner went so far as to push back on the idea that a donation from his father, Charles Kushner, played a role in his acceptance to Harvard nearly 30 years ago, but his answer literally admitted as much. 

“Kushner was admitted to Harvard, after his father pledged to donate $2.5 million—with donations beginning once his son started classes. While in college, Jared began investing in apartment buildings, many of them in Somerville, a short walk from campus,” the article read, and Kushner highlighted in his response. 

“This allegation has been repeated for nearly two decades, but that doesn’t make it true,” Kushner wrote. But just several lines later he added: “His philanthropy may have played a role in my admission.”

Turns out, Kushner isn’t disputing the line in the article at all, suggesting his family’s giving millions to Harvard may have had an impact, but he still took issue with any suggestion that he wasn’t a top high school student or lacked merit.

While Kushner did not flag the lines specifically, he was clearly triggered when The New Yorker called him a “middling student” while he attended Frisch School, with a family acquaintance saying, “He’s a parody of someone to whom everything has been given.”

“The claim that I was a mediocre student is contradicted by the contemporaneous record: I was a top student, captain of the basketball team, assistant captain of the hockey team, an award-winning debater, and finished the New York City Marathon while still in high school,” Kushner wrote. 

According to Kushner, the distortion of his record “started with a quote attributed to an administrator at my high school who later said her words had been distorted. Both she and her principal explicitly disputed the allegation in the attached letters.”

As evidence, Kushner shared two letters from 2006, which did not provide proof that he was an exemplary student, but focused on a quote about him as a student that they wrote afterward had been distorted. 

One letter was from his former high school administrator, Margot Krebs. She wrote to him that her quote in a book, as reported by the Daily News, had been “totally distorted,” though she had not seen the actual book. 

“I told him you had many personal attributes, including individuality, enterprise and great charisma, that made you a desirable candidate for Harvard,” she wrote 20 years ago.

The other letter he shared on Thursday to support his claim that his academic record had been distorted was from the principal of the Frisch School, Kalman Stein, who also raised concerns over the Daily News article about a book by Daniel Golden quoting Krebs. 

In it, he reassured Kushner that the school was “quite upset by the inaccurate and misleading content of the article and by the discomfort it might have caused you and your family.”

In the letter, Stein said he spoke to the book’s author but Kushner never came up. He also said that, had his name come up, he would have told him he never talks about students or alumni with unauthorized individuals, but he also had never met Kushner, had never crossed paths with him and knew nothing about his college path.

Stein also noted that he had spoken to Krebs about her own interview and wrote, “As she recalls, she responded that if you were not absolutely at the top of your class you did have special qualities and strengths which should have, and apparently did, make the admissions people at Harvard take notice and decide to admit you.”

As for the suggestion that his father’s donation of millions helped secure his place at Harvard, Kushner also wrote in his post, “My father’s philanthropy was not limited to Harvard.”

“For more than four decades, he has contributed over $100 million to charitable causes and institutions, including schools attended by members of our family and many institutions with which our family had no personal connection,” he wrote.

In 2025, Charles Kushner was appointed as Ambassador to France and Monaco by his son’s father-in-law, Donald Trump. The plum posting came after Trump pardoned Charles Kushner in 2020, after he pleaded guilty to counts of assisting in the filing of false tax returns, witness retaliation, and making false statements to the Federal Election Commission, and served two years in prison.

news.title: Andy Burnham gives UK update on Russia plague after scientist dies in 'test tube lab accident'
news.text: Andy Burnham has given an update following reports of a plague death in Russia . A woman in Russia died from pneumonia of "undetermined" origin after potentially being exposed to the plague. The 28-year-old woman was later identified as Darya Shipilova , who worked at the Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. Media reports in the country said some 200 people were placed in isolation following the death. Her death sparked concerns of a potential outbreak and another pandemic, just years since the world returned to seeming normality in the aftermath of Covid. British Prime Minister Burnham said he did not want to "alarm" the public and that officials would "monitor the situation closely". He addressed the concerns head-on while being quizzed by reporters during his visit to Berlin for his first official European bilateral visit. "Obviously, we take the greatest of care in relation to any issue that relates to our biosecurity, and at this point in time, while we would monitor the situation closely, I wouldn’t want to say anything further," he said. "We certainly wouldn’t want to alarm people. We will do what we can to request that the right steps are being taken, and that’s the approach we’ll take." The UK Health Security Agency said plague is not found in the UK and that the probability of a case occurring in a person returning to the country is "considered very low". Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor did not link the fatal case to the highly-transmissible pneumonic plague, saying the lab worker contracted pneumonia of "unknown" origin and that "extensive" testing found no evidence her illness was cause by any of the pathogens she worked with. "We don't understand how she was infected," said Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management. "We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow up of the questions that we have asked. "We have posed these questions to our colleagues in the Russian Federation. In fairness, they have responded. We've gone back with more questions." US President Donald Trump said he would discuss the issues ahead of his phonecall with Russian President Vladimir Putin yesterday, the despot's birthday. "They're sharing it a little bit with our people. We expect them to share it a lot with our people," Trump said.
news.summary: As many as 200 people were reportedly being placed in isolation, after the death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova when she was potentially exposed to the plague

news.title: Greg Abbott Gets Good Sign After Double Texas Polling Blow
news.text: Texas Governor Greg Abbott got some welcome news on Thursday in his reelection bid after two recent polls showed his Democratic challenger narrowly ahead. A UMass Lowell/YouGov survey of 850 likely Texas voters found Abbott leading Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa 48 percent to 44 percent. Six percent were undecided, and 1 percent backed Libertarian Pat Dixon. The poll was conducted September 18-28 and carries an adjusted margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points, so Abbott’s lead is within the margin. The result follows two polls that gave Hinojosa the edge. A New York Times/Siena College poll released Saturday had her ahead by 3 points, which was within that poll’s margin of error. A separate YouGov survey of 3,622 likely voters, fielded September 28-October 5, put Hinojosa up 48 percent to 47 percent. UMass Lowell finished its fieldwork before either of those polls did. Newsweek reached out to the Abbott and Hinojosa campaigns for comment Thursday. Eduardo Leal, a spokesperson for the Abbott campaign, told Newsweek in an email on Thursday: "We don't comment on polls, but we know that Governor Abbott's vision will beat high-tax Hinojosa." Abbott Runs Ahead of Paxton With Independents The UMass Lowell poll found Texas’ U.S. Senate race tied. Democratic state Representative James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton each drew 45 percent, with 7 percent undecided. Abbott does better than Paxton with the voters likely to settle both races. He wins 26 percent of independents, compared with 18 percent for Paxton. Among Texans who backed a third-party candidate or skipped the 2024 presidential election, Abbott takes 35 percent and Paxton's 26 percent. His supporters also appear settled. Ninety-five percent of Abbott voters said they would definitely vote for him, compared with 93 percent of Hinojosa’s backers. “The last time Democrats won a U.S. Senate race in Texas [Lloyd Bentsen in 1988], Ken Paxton didn’t yet have a law degree and James Talarico wasn’t even born," said John Cluverius, director of survey research for UMass Lowell’s Center for Public Opinion. "With the race tied, anything can happen between now and the election. Neither of the premier statewide races has a clear leader. Texas, a once-reliable rock, is starting to show some cracks.” Where Hinojosa Has the Edge Hinojosa leads independents 39 percent to 26 percent, but 21 percent of them remain undecided. She also leads among women, 47 percent to 44 percent, and among voters under 30, 46 percent to 40 percent. Black voters back her 61 percent to 23 percent, and Hispanic voters favor her 51 percent to 43 percent. College graduates support Hinojosa 52 percent to 42 percent. Abbott’s coalition is older and whiter. He wins voters 65 and older 59 percent to 37 percent, white voters 56 percent to 35 percent and voters without a four-year degree 51 percent to 38 percent. Men favor him by 12 points. Many voters are still getting to know the Democrat. Forty percent view Hinojosa favorably and 33 percent unfavorably, while 26 percent either had no opinion or had never heard of her. Abbott’s favorability stands at 48 percent, with 43 percent viewing him unfavorably. Turnout could decide it. The groups carrying Hinojosa in the YouGov poll, younger voters and Hispanic voters, tend to skip midterm elections at higher rates than the older white Texans who make up Abbott's base. And the governor has the money to stay on television through the final stretch. Costs and Trump Weigh on Republicans The poll also found some warning signs for Abbott. His job approval is 52 percent, down from 56 percent in UMass Lowell’s October 2020 Texas poll. President Donald Trump’s approval is 47 percent, and 53 percent disapprove. Fifty-nine percent of respondents said the country is on the wrong track. Fifty-six percent said paying for basics like housing, food and medical care has become harder over the past six months. Voters blamed Washington for energy costs. Seventy-two percent named the Iran war as the main reason for higher fuel and utility prices, and 11 percent pointed to tariffs. Sixty-nine percent said the U.S. is spending too much on the war. “When voters connect rising costs at home with specific government policies, those concerns can become politically consequential, potentially punishing the party in power,” said Rodrigo Castro Cornejo, the center’s associate director. AI data centers came up as another pressure point. Sixty-five percent oppose building one in their own community, and 56 percent support a statewide ban on building or expanding data centers in Texas. A September ReconMR/Siena poll found that voters preferred Hinojosa to Abbott on managing data center construction, 45 percent to 42 percent. What Earlier Polls Show Pollsters have traded leads all fall. A year ago, few Texas Republicans would have predicted that Abbott, who has won each of his three races for governor by double digits, would be scrapping for votes less than four weeks before Election Day. Recent surveys, however, suggest that the race has become a true toss-up. A YouGov poll of 3,622 likely voters, conducted September 28-October 5, found Hinojosa narrowly ahead 48 percent to 47 percent, with 5 percent undecided. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points. The shift is especially striking compared with polling earlier this year. In June, a New York Times/Siena College poll of 656 likely voters found Abbott leading 51 percent to 44 percent. But when the Times/Siena returned to the field September 21-30, Hinojosa had moved ahead 49 percent to 46 percent among 615 likely voters. A Marist University survey September 17-20 among 1,139 registered voters produced the same 49-46 result. Other recent polls point to a similar reversal. ReconMR and the Siena Research Institute found Hinojosa leading 49 percent to 45 percent, a turnaround from July, when the same poll had Abbott ahead by a point. Not every survey shows Hinojosa in front, however. A Fox News poll conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24-28 put Abbott ahead 52 percent to 47 percent among 881 likely voters. Big Data Poll and Slingshot Strategies also showed the governor with mid-single-digit leads, as did a Stratus Intelligence survey commissioned by the Republican group Texans for a Conservative Majority. Between those competing findings are polls showing an essentially deadlocked race. An N+ Univision/YouGov survey found both candidates at 47 percent, while an Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation poll gave Abbott an edge, 46.9 percent to 45.8 percent. The contrast from the summer is stark. Abbott led by 7 points in a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll in early June, and a late-July Texas Southern University survey found him ahead 49 percent to 43 percent. No public poll since mid-September has shown him leading by more than 5 points. Blue Texas? It Might Happen Hinojosa's fate may be tied to Talarico's. A Senate race that drives Democratic-leaning voters to the polls would help her more than anything her own campaign can buy. Democrats have been promising a breakthrough in Texas for three decades. No Democrat has won statewide office there since 1994 [Kay Hutchison, U.S. Senate], and Trump carried the state by 13 points in 2024. Abbott beat Beto O'Rourke by roughly 11 points in 2022. Hinojosa is a different kind of candidate than O'Rourke. A civil rights and union lawyer who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, she made her name in the Texas House as the chief antagonist of Abbott's school voucher push, and her campaign has since widened its focus to grocery bills, data centers and what she calls corruption in the governor's office. "Every poll tells the same story: Texans are tired of working more and getting less," Hinojosa said during the summer. Her numbers among Hispanic voters, a group that shifted sharply toward Republicans in 2024, could prove decisive. Mike Madrid, a longtime Latino political strategist, said many analysts in Washington misread the results of that election. "Most people were thinking it was part of this permanent realignment. A lot of people who understand the Latino vote were saying it's not that at all," Madrid told Newsweek. Independents are also drifting her way, according to ReconMR, which found her with large leads in Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth and San Antonio and Abbott ahead in rural areas. Abbott keeps the upper hand on the issues Republicans have run on for a decade. On securing the border, voters picked him over Hinojosa 53 percent to 39 percent, and he led on keeping Texans safe, while she led on making prices more affordable. He also has far more money. At the end of June, Abbott had about $67 million on hand to Hinojosa's $3 million, though she has said her campaign raised $20 million since January. What Happens Next Abbott’s campaign has publicly brushed off the tight numbers. His top strategist called one recent poll showing Hinojosa ahead by 3 points “bogus,” and Abbott has said his internal polling looks different. He still has a major financial advantage, although it has narrowed. Abbott outspent Hinojosa 6-to-1 from July to late September. He ended the reporting period with $18.2 million on hand, compared with Hinojosa’s $4 million, after starting the year with more than $105 million. More than 70 Latino Democratic leaders have urged the Democratic Governors Association to put $10 million into the race. Hinojosa has accepted an October 15 debate in Fort Worth. Her campaign said Abbott let the deadline pass. Early voting runs October 19-30 and Election Day is November 3. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Texas Governor Greg Abbott got some welcome news on Thursday after two recent polls showed his Democratic challenger ahead.

news.title: Judge seems poised to reinforce block of Trump's White House media ban
news.text: A federal judge appeared inclined to extend his block on President Donald Trump's ban on three media outlets from the White House. The administration's argument that the ban was based on national security concerns is contradicted by the president's own words, US District Judge Timothy Kelly said during a hearing Thursday. "That's an uphill climb," Kelly said of the Justice Department's effort to defend the ban on national security grounds, noting Trump's claim that his ban was based on his disapproval of the outlets' coverage. Kelly is weighing whether to grant a lengthier block of Trump's move to ban POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House. The Trump-appointed judge already lifted the ban last month, issuing a two-week restraining order, which he extended through Tuesday, that enabled the three organizations to regain access to the West Wing. But he now appears to be leaning toward a more durable injunction that would maintain the outlets' access during what could be months of litigation. Kelly's original ruling found that the ban likely violated the news outlets' due process rights, since the White House restricted access without any notice and without setting out any identifiable standards for news organizations to follow to maintain their credentials. "That's probably the biggest hurdle you all have," Kelly told the government during a hearing that drew a swath of media executives, reporters and First Amendment attorneys to the federal courthouse in Washington, D.C., leading Kelly to remark on the vastly outnumbered Justice Department attorney assigned to the case. In what has been a recurring theme in court battles across the country, Kelly pointed out that Trump's own comments — declaring repeatedly in interviews and on social media that he banned the outlets for writing "negative" stories about him — conflicted with the Justice Department's later efforts to claim the ban was a response to the outlets' publication of sensitive national security information. A lawyer for the news organizations, Theodore Boutrous Jr., urged Kelly to reject Trump's ban for a second reason: a violation of news organizations' First Amendment rights and an effort to chill the free press. Boutrous argued that a recent interview Trump gave to Time magazine "amounts to a confession" from the president that he revoked the journalists' press passes because he considered their stories to be too negative. "That interview really is the coup de grace," Boutrous said. He also pointed to a recent comment from Attorney General Todd Blanche that Trump banned the outlets from the White House due to their "one-sided reporting." Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik argued that the Trump administration had, in fact, provided due process to the news outlets — after Trump's ban went into effect. He cited unsigned letters from the White House press office delivered in the days after the lawsuit was filed, identifying a handful of stories the administration viewed as "misinformation" or "national security" risks. Velchik argued that the outlets "defaulted" by failing to respond to those letters. He also repeatedly attributed the letters to Trump himself, even though they were unsigned and Trump never referred to them publicly. Boutrous, calling this after-the-fact effort a "sham process," underscored the absence of any indication Trump had signed off on — or even had any awareness of — the letters. Velchik also repeatedly argued that the courts should give the president more leeway than might apply in other contexts, where decisions about reporters' access are made by federal agencies. "The White House is a sacred place," Velchik said. Kelly asked whether the president could ban a news organization from the White House based on stories that were demonstrably false. Boutrous said no, while Velchik articulated a more malleable standard. "From our perspective, it's within the discretion of the president," Velchik said. Kelly emphasized that his assessment of the issue was constrained by longstanding precedents that forbid the White House from barring access to the West Wing press areas based on disagreements with content, along with requirements that revoking such access must be based on clear standards and potential consequences spelled out in advance. The Justice Department has said it disagrees with those decisions, but the judge made clear he is bound to follow them. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.
news.summary: "That's an uphill climb," US District Judge Timothy Kelly said of the Justice Department's effort to defend the ban on national security grounds.

news.title: Republicans Blame Trump for High Costs in Two Key Senate Battlegrounds
news.text: Many Republicans in Iowa and Ohio are blaming President Donald Trump’s policies for rising costs ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to a new CNN/SSRS poll released Thursday. Fifty percent of Iowa Republicans and 49 percent of Ohio Republicans said Trump’s policies “increased the cost of living” in the new poll, which comes as the two states emerge as critical midterm battlegrounds despite the states backing Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Both states have competitive Senate and governor’s races in this year’s midterms. Control of the House and Senate could come down to these two Midwestern states. Both are former battlegrounds, having given their electoral votes to former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012 before shifting rightward during the Trump era. Trump’s inroads with white, rural voters helped move these states to the Republican column. But Democrats believe dissatisfaction with the economy during Trump’s second term in office could give them the opportunity to win back voters to make the states competitive again this year. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats when the president’s approval rating is low, and recent polls have found Trump’s numbers falling to their lowest point of his second term, fueling Democrats’ optimism about their chances of competing in states like Iowa and Ohio. The economy has become a “significant drag on Republican prospects” because there is a “very close link” to how people feel about their personal finances and how they vote in elections, Costas Panagopoulos, professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Newsweek. “If even the president's own supporters are blaming him for these issues, there's the likelihood that they will either defect to Democratic candidates in the midterms or not vote at all, which could be equally problematic,” he said. “Voters are connecting the dots.” Cultural issues, which have been used as “wedge issues” in campaigns, have become “secondary” to the “economic pain” voters are dealing with in this election, he said. In Iowa, Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek are competing in a Senate race, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn are running in the gubernatorial race. Ohio races are also highly competitive. In the Senate race, Republican Senator Jon Husted is facing a challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Meanwhile, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton are running in the gubernatorial race. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Newsweek that nobody “can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement.” “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” he said. Iowa and Ohio Voters Blame Trump Policies for Rising Prices Across all voter groups, 74 percent of voters in Iowa and 76 percent of voters in Ohio believe Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living, according to the new polls from CNN. Fifty-five percent in Iowa and 58 percent in Ohio said they believe that Trump’s tariffs are a “bad thing” for their state, while 70 percent in Iowa and 68 percent in Ohio said the recent increase in gas prices, which have soared amid the Iran war, has caused personal hardship for them. Both polls were conducted from September 29 to October 5. The Iowa poll surveyed 801 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points, while the Ohio poll surveyed 760 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Trump won both states by double digits in the 2024 election. He won Ohio by about 11 points and Iowa by about 13 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris. What Polls Show About Iowa, Ohio Races The polls pointed to competitive races in both states. Hinson held a 2-point lead in the Iowa Senate race over Turek, 45 percent to 43 percent. However, in the gubernatorial race, Sand held a 9-point lead over Lahn, 51 percent to 42 percent. Democrats had an advantage in both statewide races in Ohio. Brown led Husted by 6 points, 49 percent to 43 percent, in the Senate race, while Acton held an 8-point lead, 50 percent to 42 percent, over Ramaswamy in the gubernatorial race, according to the poll. The economic fallout of Trump’s policies gives Democrats a chance to persuade some Republicans to vote for their candidates, but Democrats should not necessarily expect to win “large segments of the Republican population,” Panagopoulos said. Its impact on turnout will be critically important, he said. “What we're seeing is lots of enthusiasm in this election cycle around Democrats, around the prospects of winning in November and putting the brakes on some of these Republican policies,” he said. “That enthusiasm often translates into higher turnout amongst those voters in elections. We're seeing comparatively lower levels of enthusiasm among Republicans.” Why Iowa and Ohio Appear Competitive Again These two former battlegrounds appear competitive in this election cycle as Democrats hope to expand the electoral playing field into more conservative states. The economy is a central reason Democrats believe these states may be competitive. Voter beliefs that Trump’s policies have driven up the cost of living and that tariffs are hurting their states could weaken Republicans in the states. Republicans have long held an advantage over Democrats in terms of voter perceptions of the economy, and Americans often vote based on economic conditions, so a shift in that perception could leave the GOP more vulnerable in places they’ve performed well in recent elections. Trump has done well with white voters in rural areas in both states. This voting bloc was previously more competitive, but the Democratic collapse among them has been a main factor driving them into Republican control. Democrats have gained ground in suburban areas in those states, but have not made strong enough inroads to offset their rural losses. Democrats have struggled statewide in both of these states. Sand and Brown are among the only Democrats who have managed to win statewide races in either state during the Trump era. Sand and Brown running again in 2026, a more favorable national environment, has bolstered Democrats’ hopes of flipping those states. Iowa is a major agricultural exporter of goods like corn and soybeans, and farmers may feel the squeeze from tariffs and diesel prices. Meanwhile, data centers have become a sticking point in Ohio especially, tying into broader themes of affordability that have defined the midterms. The Senate races in these two states are especially important. Democrats are hoping to flip control of the chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, but have limited pickup opportunities in traditionally competitive states. This means they need to compete in double-digit Trump states to win a majority. As these two states do have a history of backing Democrats as recently as the 2010s, they have become some of the most hotly contested races that could ultimately decide whether Democrats or Republicans win control of the Senate after the midterms. Donald Trump Approval Rating Trump’s approval rating was also underwater in both states. In Iowa, his approval stood at -17 points, 41 percent approving and 58 percent disapproving of his job performance. Over in Ohio, his net approval rating was -28 points, with 36 percent approving and 64 percent disapproving. Two recent national polls shed light on Trump’s standing nationwide. Only 36 percent of Americans approved of Trump, while 64 percent disapproved of him, in a new Reuters/Ipsos poll of 3,526 registered voters. Meanwhile, his approval stood at 38 percent, with 60 percent disapproving of him, in a new YouGov/The Economist poll of 1,381 registered voters. His approval among Republicans was still strong in both of those polls. Seventy-seven percent of Republicans in the Reuters/Ipsos poll and 79 percent of Republicans in the YouGov poll approved of Trump. The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted from September 30 to October 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.7 percentage points among registered voters. The YouGov poll was conducted from October 2 to 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. What Happens Next Trump’s standing among Republicans will have major implications for the midterms. The president will want to retain positive numbers with his core base of supporters to ensure they head to the polls. Issues like the economy, cost of living and gas prices could impact how Americans view his presidency. Panagopoulos said it is likely too late for Republicans to change the narrative about the economy. “Millions of votes have already been cast. These views are baked in the minds of the electorate at this point and what they can do is focus on mobilizing supporters to get to the polls,” he said.
news.summary: Republicans are blaming Trump policies for increasing the cost of living in Iowa and Ohio, a new poll found ahead of the midterms.

news.title: Operation Epic Fury is an epic failure at home and in Hormuz
news.text: Speaking before the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, US President Donald Trump laid bare the existential crossroads facing Washington’s seven-month campaign against Iran. Framing the conflict as a choice between signing a post-midterm diplomatic deal or initiating total annihilation, his rhetoric underscored a troubling reality: Operation Epic Fury, launched jointly with Israel in late February 2026, has been an Epic Failure. Far from delivering the swift, decisive outcome intended, it has created a humiliating stalemate, with global ramifications for the US’s uncertain place in the world and domestic implications for the ruling party in the US. What Washington planned as a high-intensity decapitation effort targeting Tehran’s ballistic missile infrastructure and naval assets has instead evolved into a grinding, multipolar war of attrition. The US now finds itself caught between an unwinnable air campaign and an unpalatable political compromise, while the global economy buckles under the fallout.The core vulnerability in the American war effort stems from a fundamental operational mismatch. Unwilling to commit ground troops to a costly land occupation, a step the administration remains reluctant to contemplate for understandable domestic reasons, the US military relies on air dominance and standoff strikes, whose limitations are all too apparent. While stationary infrastructure and conventional naval installations in Iran have been degraded, airpower alone cannot eliminate Iran’s distributed, deeply buried, and asymmetric capabilities..Tehran has also successfully broadened the theatre of operations far beyond its own borders. Houthi forces in Yemen have effectively choked commercial transit through the Bab al-Mandab, turning the Southern Red Sea into an operational hazard zone, while Iranian-aligned Shia militias in Iraq have executed drone and missile strikes against critical regional energy infrastructure, including Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline.When Saudi leaders requested US air defence coverage to shield these vital supply routes, Washington demurred, constrained by a need to preserve its own dwindling supply of precision-guided munitions.This refusal highlights a growing operational crisis within the Pentagon. Seven months of near-continuous combat sorties and high-rate missile defence interceptions have severely drawn down US and allied inventories of long-range precision strike systems, exposing the severe limitations of the Western defence industrial base. The economic fallout of this strategic impasse extends far beyond West Asia. With transit through the Strait of Hormuz severely restricted and regional pipelines damaged, benchmark crude oil prices have again surged past $100, having hit a recent high of $114 five months ago. This sustained energy shock has reintroduced severe inflationary pressures into the world’s economies, squeezing consumers and creating significant political headwinds ahead of the US midterm elections..For global markets, the ongoing hostilities have triggered a profound supply-side energy shock. With the physical blockade of Hormuz choking off roughly 20 percent of global petroleum transit and liquefied natural gas shipments, elevated crude prices have spiked shipping freight costs, doubled energy transit insurance premiums, and forced global central banks to abruptly halt planned interest rate cuts to combat reignited inflationary pressures. Few major nations bear this macroeconomic strain more acutely than India. Highly exposed due to our dependence on foreign energy to fulfil over 85 percent of crude-oil requirements, India faces a sharp widening of its current account deficit (where every $10 surge in crude prices expands the trade deficit by roughly 0.5 percent of GDP) alongside persistent downward pressure on the Indian rupee, which has hit historic lows beyond ₹95 to a US dollar.The severe disruption of Gulf trade corridors has simultaneously squeezed input margins across Indian manufacturing, chemical and aviation sectors, compounded by higher import bills for fertilisers and essential commodities, while stoking domestic retail inflation through heightened transportation logistics. The conflict poses a direct threat to India’s broader growth trajectory, threatening to trim our expected GDP expansion if high energy costs remain entrenched.Meanwhile, Washington’s heavy reliance on secondary financial sanctions, has accelerated a structural shift in global finance. Member nations at the BRICS summit in New Delhi emphasised creating alternative non-dollar settlement systems to shield domestic economies from unilateral American leverage..Concurrently, European central banks, including those of France and Norway, have quietly begun repatriating gold reserves from Federal Reserve vaults in New York back to continental Europe, reflecting a historic erosion of trust in American financial stewardship. Far from triggering the immediate collapse of the Iranian state, the conflict has consolidated Tehran’s domestic political control. By demonstrating an ability to withstand direct bombardment while disrupting roughly 20 percent of global daily oil transit, Tehran has projected an image of regional defiance that has altered diplomatic calculations.Elevated oil prices have provided windfall revenues to Moscow to fund operations in Ukraine, while Beijing monitors American failures with a keen strategic eye on the balance of power in the Indo-Pacific. Realising that US security guarantees are constrained, traditional American partners in the Gulf have even initiated direct bilateral discussions with Tehran to manage local stability. Beyond the immediate economic fallout, the impasse severely erodes global confidence in the US as a predictable policymaker and reliable security guarantor. By initiating a major conflict without a coherent off-ramp, and subsequently being unable to provide protection for critical energy corridors due to depleted ammunition stockpiles, Washington has demonstrated both the volatile unpredictability of its foreign policy and its operational limits..This stark gap between American strategic commitments and actual ability to sustain them is forcing all nations to diversify their security relationships, hedging against a superpower whose promises increasingly seem subject to domestic political whims and constrained military resources.The war between the US and Iran has settled into a dangerous, unstable equilibrium. Washington possesses overwhelming destructive capacity, yet lacks the strategic leverage or political willingness to enforce a decisive outcome. Tehran lacks the capability to win conventionally, but retains sufficient asymmetric reach to hold its own against US attacks.As military stockpiles run low and global markets adjust to prolonged instability, the Iran War serves as a stark demonstration of the limits of unilateral military force in an increasingly multipolar world.Shashi Tharoor | Lok Sabha MP, Chair of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and Sahitya Akademi-winning author (Views are personal)(office@tharoor.in).Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: DNC Sues Trump Administration Over Taxpayer-Funded Ads
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its taxpayer-funded advertisements that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, alleging the ads violate federal laws on government spending and propaganda.

The DNC cited a measure Trump signed into law this year that says funds appropriated by Congress can’t be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

The lawsuit also cites the Anti-Deficiency Act, which bars spending government money that hasn’t been appropriated by Congress, and the Purpose Statute, which says taxpayer funds can be used only for the specific purposes approved by Congress.

The DNC said the administration’s use of taxpayer dollars for “campaign-style advertisements” deprived Democrats “of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates.” The use of public funds places Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, it argued.

The watchdog group Common Cause filed its own suit making similar legal arguments, alleging the administration had violated appropriations statutes.

The ads, launched last month, sparked criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, many of whom questioned their legality.

Trump reversed course Monday, announcing on Truth Social he would no longer use government funds for the ads and saying he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would foot the bill moving forward, instead. He didn’t say whether the government would be reimbursed for the ads that already ran.
news.author: Jeff Charles

news.title: 'He's Got Nothing to Lose': Trump Advised by Disgraced Election Clerk to Seize Ballots as Republicans Looking at 'Nightmare' Midterms
news.text:
President Donald Trump, who previously expressed doubts about election results, was advised by Tina Peters, a convicted former Colorado election clerk, to seize ballots and perform a hand recount, RadarOnline.com has learned. 

MAGA Republicans' concern as the midterm elections grow near has increased, with some suggesting the midterms could be a bloodbath.Donald Trump Advised to Recount Ballots by HandTrump reportedly met with Peters on Monday, October 5, per former Justice Department official Ed Martin.

He told conservative network Real America's Voice, "And so when Tina Peters, you know, famous Colorado clerk, was in the Oval Office today, just two hours ago, talking about this question, the president's taking it seriously. If the Congress won't pass the SAVE America Act, and they won't, then the president's gonna have to do what he's gonna do."

Martin, Trump's former pardon attorney, added, "And it is not a local issue when it's national security, and it's clearly national security."

However, the president's team did not confirm the meeting. Spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement the White House does "not comment on private meetings that may or may not have happened."Tina Peters' Offered Commutation on SentencePeters worked as a Mesa County clerk and was convicted in 2024 of multiple felonies after having a hand in a security breach of election equipment.

Peters was released in June 2026 after her sentence was shortened by Governor Jared Polis.

In a statement after her commutation letter was delivered, Polis said, “I made mistakes, and for those I am sorry. Five years ago I misled the Secretary of State when allowing a person to gain access to county voting equipment. That was wrong. I have learned and grown during my time in prison, and going forward I will make sure that my actions always follow the law, and I will avoid the mistakes of the past.”Tina Peters' Attorney Backs PlanPeters' attorney, Peter Ticktin, backed the clerk's alleged plan, believing the likelihood of an administrative intervention was high. 

He told Colorado podcaster Joe Oltmann, "In the event that we have this kind of a disaster and everything goes wrong, and the vote is crazy, and the senatorial races put enough there to remove the president and the vice president, if that nightmare should come true, Donald Trump is not going to relinquish control again."

Due to the country's high tension, Ticktin concluded Trump "has nothing to lose," indicating the same goes for the country at large. He suggested a civil war might be on the horizon, and he'd rather "it'd be marching off with our side and all of the armaments."

Despite Ticktin's supportive position of Peters alleged beliefs, his publicist claimed he was not allowed to divulge further about any potential meeting with the president.'There Are Targets'During the conversation with Peters' attorney, podcaster Oltmann offered his support for the plan. Oltmann previously stated, "Violence is going to be necessary" and "There are targets."

Oltmann is known for calling for the execution of Colorado's top Democrats.
news.summary: President Donald Trump reportedly met with a disgraced election clerk regarding plans for the upcoming midterm elections.

news.title: Mike Tyson says he delivered letter from Sean 'Diddy' Combs to Donald Trump
news.text:
Mike Tyson is revealing the big favor Sean "Diddy" Combs asked of him from behind bars.

During a Thursday, Oct. 8, appearance on SiriusXM’s "Andy Cohen Live," the former boxer, 60, opened up about the status of his friendship with the disgraced music mogul, who is currently serving a 50-month prison sentence for his July 2025 sex-crimes conviction.

"I'm friendly with Puff," Tyson said, referring to Combs by one of his many stage names. Host Andy Cohen then asked, "Were you surprised by what happened with him?"

"Listen, I was surprised that they went through so many lengths to get him," the athlete replied. "They used a 110-year-old rule to get him – that case 110 years ago, but they used it to get him. Can you imagine that?"

Combs was accused of leading a criminal enterprise where he coerced victims into participating in sex parties, known as "freak offs," often involving travel across state and international boundaries. His two-month trial last year ended in a mixed verdict.

While the jury acquitted him of trafficking and racketeering charges, they found him guilty of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution, citing his violation of the 1910 Mann Act, which criminalizes the transport of “any woman or girl for the purpose of prostitution or debauchery, or for any other immoral purpose.”

Combs has denied all allegations of sexual misconduct and has been trying to appeal his conviction since the case concluded.

Tyson, who has voiced his support for Combs in the past, revealed on "Andy Cohen Live" that he and the rapper have been in touch during his incarceration.

"I spoke with him once on the phone," Tyson revealed. "He wanted me to give a letter to the president."

"And did you give a letter to the president from him?" Cohen asked, to which Tyson confirmed, "I did what he told me to do, yeah."

In January, President Donald Trump said he received a letter from Combs asking for a pardon, which could be the letter Tyson delivered, but he said he would not grant the request.

Trump previously addressed the conviction in an August 2025 interview with Newsmax, saying, "I was very friendly with him. I got along with him great."

"[He] seemed like a nice guy," Trump continued. "I didn't know him well, but when I ran for office he was very hostile."

Combs, who still faces upward of 70 civil lawsuits nationwide, remains behind bars at New Jersey's FCI Fort Dix. His release date has moved multiple times, most recently being pushed back from Jan. 21, 2028, to March 2, 2028, after an NBC News report alleging the hip-hop producer has fellow inmates cook and clean for him, give him massages, and has access to outside alcohol and a cellphone, which are considered contraband.

news.title: Joe Rogan Gets Staggering Payday in New Podcast Deal
news.text:
Podcaster Joe Rogan has re-upped his lucrative podcast deal with Spotify. 

The deal is similar to his previous one, as The Joe Rogan Experience will be distributed broadly for a staggering $250 million, The Wall Street Journal reported.

“The partnership with Spotify has been an amazing fit, and they’re incredible to work with,” Rogan said. “I’m extremely happy and excited to continue with them for years to come.”

The Joe Rogan Experience has been No. 1 on Edison Research’s list of the most listened-to podcasts in the U.S. since tracking began in 2019. The show has more than 18 million followers on Spotify, and more than 21 million on YouTube.

His show reached about 28.4 million Americans in the second quarter of this year, according to Edison data.

Since first entering a deal with Rogan in 2020, Spotify has remained largely hands-off with the show, letting Rogan and his team take editorial control.

“Joe has built something incredibly enduring, and his show continues to resonate with a massive global audience because there’s simply nothing else like it,” Jordan Newman, Spotify’s head of content partnerships, said.

Rogan, a former independent-turned-MAGA, was a part of the so-called “podcast bros” credited with helping to get President Donald Trump elected in the last election, as their shows appeal to younger, male audiences. 

But Rogan has grown very critical of the president in recent weeks, criticizing Trump’s immigration tactics and his disastrous war with Iran. 

He has said the war in particular made Trump’s MAGA base feel “betrayed,” as Trump made starting “no new wars” a pillar of his 2024 presidential campaign.

In what may be a clue as to where Trump voters are headed in the next presidential election cycle, Rogan has been heaping praise on Vice President JD Vance, calling him “f---ing amazing” and a “masterclass” in public speaking.

“He’s so good,” the podcaster said in March. “He’s great. Thank God for that guy. He’s so good at dismantling those dopey people.”
